articles.title: Palmer Luckey thinks China is ‘thrilled to have Jensen out,’ so he wants the ousted Nvidia CEO reinstated
articles.body:
Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey thinks Nvidia’s board is giving China exactly what it wants by removing the company’s longtime CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang.
Nvidia, the leading semiconductor designer whose chips power much of the AI industry, is undergoing a critical, unexpected leadership change. Huang, who led the company for 33 years, stepped down last week amid several controversies, including his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy who has been investigated for possibly smuggling Nvidia chips into China to circumvent U.S. export restrictions.
“China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, repeating a statement he posted on X last week. “They’re thrilled to have Jensen out… There’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know it makes America weaker to knock him out.”
Luckey disagrees with Huang’s longstanding position that Nvidia should have more leeway to export chips to China. But he also recognizes that China stands to benefit if its domestic chipmakers can challenge Nvidia’s dominance.
“China doesn’t want Nvidia to sell GPUs to Chinese companies,” Luckey said. “There are Chinese companies that want to buy Nvidia GPUs… China will not give them an import permit because they want to build an internal domestic processor industry… not build one that is dependent on the United States.”
Nvidia has said as much itself — the U.S. government granted the company license to ship some of its powerful H200 chips to certain Chinese customers, but those sales were restricted by the Chinese government. Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress said during the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that it will no longer sell H200 chips in China at all.
Luckey is far from alone among industry peers in his defense of Huang.
More than 200,000 people — including Elon Musk and the CEOs of Y Combinator, Databricks, Epic Games, Shopify, and Replit — have signed a petition calling for Nvidia to reinstate its founder. But Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that the company does not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.

articles.title: Nvidia clarifies when it will — and won’t —keep financing neoclouds
articles.body:
One reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it.
And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter, which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter.
But Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the company aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance new data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, announced in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company said.
Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking. She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion.
Under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the company is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she said.
“There is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and or debt, in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” Kress said to analysts on Tuesday during the quarterly conference call.
She pointed to OpenAI PORTS-Pike campus as an example of where such terms apply. When asked, she also said this wasn’t a change in policy, but simply a clarification of existing terms. However, these disclosures have never been public before.
Kress also made clear that Nvidia wasn’t bailing on all the ways it was financing the AI boom, especially new data centers. But, she said, Nvidia was going to be far more selective in the future.
“The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That’s a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities,” she said. At the same time, she insisted that Nvidia was “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing.”
One of the ongoing criticisms Huang faced was his love of circular deals: invest in his customers so they would turn around and buy his products. Kress is now trying to strike a delicate balance. She isn’t saying she will pull the rug out from under Nvidia’s customers. After all, the company’s investments undoubtedly spurred the AI boom that has been so lucrative for Nvidia. But she’s also signaling that the days of Huang’s freewheeling dealmaking may be over.

articles.title: Google Gemini's "Tasks" Personal Assistant Is Now Free
articles.body:
Put Gemini to work for you
The best assistant knows you and helps you get things done. Today, you can now hand off even more tasks to Gemini and move on with your day. We’ve built it for anyone who has tasks piling up during all the classes, meetings, and school drop-offs that fill the day. Our goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.
Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. We’re also rolling out a set of advanced features, starting in the U.S.
How it’s changing my daily routine
If your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards are already in the Google ecosystem, Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because this sensitive data already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.
Here’s how I’m using it.
Recently, our minivan’s check-engine light came on. Ugh. I pulled out Gemini and told it, "Our minivan is overdue for a service appointment. Please call the two nearest dealerships and figure out how to get an appointment early Friday morning over the next month or so."
Because Gemini already knows we drive a 2019 Honda Odyssey and where we live through Personal Intelligence, it found the nearest shops on Google Maps and called both at once 1 . Thankfully, I didn’t have to suffer through any hold music. Gemini did the job, found a time in my Google Calendar when I was free, and added the Friday early morning appointment in less than five minutes. Done. (On the dealership's end, Gemini disclosed right away that it's an AI. Businesses can opt out whenever they want, and Gemini won’t give out my payment or private account info unless I say so.)
In the background, Gemini called both dealerships at once, sat through the hold music for me, booked an appointment at the shop that accepts appointments vs. walk-ins only, and put Friday's appointment on my calendar without me having to check it.
Last month it saved us real money after we got hit with a surprise $389 electric bill. I gave Gemini permission to access our utility portal with the new Google Password Manager integration and asked for it to analyze our past billing statements in my email. Gemini worked for a few minutes, and then nailed it. The primary culprit was our heat pump, which it turns out was kicking on around 4 p.m., right in the middle of peak pricing. My wife and I never would have caught that digging through the PDFs and emails ourselves.
I use it for smaller stuff, too. For our upcoming holiday trip back to Oklahoma, I recently asked Gemini to give me the best options for a USB-C charger. Gemini quickly compared chargers thanks to Google’s Shopping Graph, asked me follow-up questions about the wattage and color, and then helped me check out using the new Google Pay integration. The best part: it also found a discount code so I saved an extra $10. Done.
Gemini now uses the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) to make purchases like this. We’re working with American Express (coming soon), Mastercard, and Visa to keep your purchases secure with digital tokens on supported cards. And when you shop with Gemini, you still earn your card's points, cashback, or purchase protections during checkout. You can also set a hard spending cap upfront, and Gemini is designed to stay within your budget. All of your receipts and tracking info land straight in Google Wallet, which is expanding to iOS starting today. Up next, we’ll integrate the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) into Gemini so everyone can expect an even faster and more reliable shopping experience from discovery to checkout.
Gemini lets you set the spending limit and still earn every airline mile, cashback point, and perk on your card.
Gemini helps with weeknight dinners, too. I recently stared down a nearly empty fridge rushing out the door in the morning, and I texted Gemini with the new RCS integration 2 : “Add lasagna, strawberries, cucumbers, and vanilla ice cream to our Instacart order.” On the walk out, I saw an empty Cheerios box in the pantry, so I snapped a photo and sent a quick follow-up: “Add this too.” Gemini added it, and then handed me off to Instacart to complete the order. Groceries were on the doorstep when we got home. Done. Today, Gemini connects with more than 60 popular apps and, as a developer, you can apply to join our Connected Apps Platform.
My wife and I also use Gemini to sort out medical bills, keep track of insurance renewals, and stay on top of our kids' schedules. Earlier this week, I forwarded a batch of school emails from Gmail to gemini@google.com. In less than a minute, every date was on my calendar with my wife invited. Better yet, it noticed a conflict during basketball practice and asked if I wanted to text one of the other parents to trade carpool duty.
How we protect your data
As Gemini becomes more capable, we continually advance our security defenses. When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users. Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams. This sandbox is just one of multiple layers of defense, including prompt-injection filters that scan search results, webpages, and more alongside Google Safe Browsing to limit which links Gemini can open.
As Gemini works on a task, you can jump in to give it more instructions at any point, and it’s also designed to pause and check with you before critical steps. For example, Gemini is designed to ask for your confirmation or pre-approval before clicking "Buy," and will ask clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous. For routine stuff you already trust, like adding those Cheerios to your grocery cart, you can set that to “Always allow” so it doesn’t pester you.
And finally, we give you access to settings and tools that help you safeguard your data and protect your privacy. You can adjust task settings, disconnect Google and third-party apps, or delete chat history anytime. For a closer look at how we’ve implemented a multi-layer defense-in-depth security strategy, read our technical paper.
And please participate in our bug bounty program through Google’s AI Vulnerability Reward Program (AI VRP) to advance the security of agentic systems.
How you can help us improve
While we’ve tested tasks extensively to minimize mistakes, we haven't eliminated all of them. You may encounter situations where a task fails to complete or misses the mark. When you see this, please provide feedback by giving the response a “thumbs down.”
For example, the way personal assistants navigate the web is still evolving as sites are still adapting to these new use cases. On some sites, Gemini can make it most of the way through and then hand the screen back to you to click the final button. We’re partnering directly with major websites and security providers to help the web evolve so it works well for site owners and personal assistants. For decades, bots were blocked by default because most were malicious. Personal assistants require a more nuanced approach, and we believe open, verifiable standards will benefit everyone.
How to try it
Ready to hand off your next task? Open Gemini, flip the home-screen toggle from Chat to Task, and tell Gemini what you need done. Starting in the U.S., you can also forward emails to gemini@google.com or text Gemini by following these instructions:
- Open Gemini on Android or iOS and tap Settings
- Tap Channels
- Tap Set up under Text with Gemini
- Verify your phone number
We can’t wait to see what Gemini crosses off your list first.

Gemini lets you set the spending limit and still earn every airline mile, cashback point, and perk on your card.
Gemini helps with weeknight dinners, too. I recently stared down a nearly empty fridge rushing out the door in the morning, and I texted Gemini with the new RCS integration 2 : “Add lasagna, strawberries, cucumbers, and vanilla ice cream to our Instacart order.” On the walk out, I saw an empty Cheerios box in the pantry, so I snapped a photo and sent a quick follow-up: “Add this too.” Gemini added it, and then handed me off to Instacart to complete the order. Groceries were on the doorstep when we got home. Done. Today, Gemini connects with more than 60 popular apps and, as a developer, you can apply to join our Connected Apps Platform.
My wife and I also use Gemini to sort out medical bills, keep track of insurance renewals, and stay on top of our kids' schedules. Earlier this week, I forwarded a batch of school emails from Gmail to gemini@google.com. In less than a minute, every date was on my calendar with my wife invited. Better yet, it noticed a conflict during basketball practice and asked if I wanted to text one of the other parents to trade carpool duty.
How we protect your data
As Gemini becomes more capable, we continually advance our security defenses. When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users. Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams. This sandbox is just one of multiple layers of defense, including prompt-injection filters that scan search results, webpages, and more alongside Google Safe Browsing to limit which links Gemini can open.
As Gemini works on a task, you can jump in to give it more instructions at any point, and it’s also designed to pause and check with you before critical steps. For example, Gemini is designed to ask for your confirmation or pre-approval before clicking "Buy," and will ask clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous. For routine stuff you already trust, like adding those Cheerios to your grocery cart, you can set that to “Always allow” so it doesn’t pester you.
And finally, we give you access to settings and tools that help you safeguard your data and protect your privacy. You can adjust task settings, disconnect Google and third-party apps, or delete chat history anytime. For a closer look at how we’ve implemented a multi-layer defense-in-depth security strategy, read our technical paper.
And please participate in our bug bounty program through Google’s AI Vulnerability Reward Program (AI VRP) to advance the security of agentic systems.
How you can help us improve
While we’ve tested tasks extensively to minimize mistakes, we haven't eliminated all of them. You may encounter situations where a task fails to complete or misses the mark. When you see this, please provide feedback by giving the response a “thumbs down.”
For example, the way personal assistants navigate the web is still evolving as sites are still adapting to these new use cases. On some sites, Gemini can make it most of the way through and then hand the screen back to you to click the final button. We’re partnering directly with major websites and security providers to help the web evolve so it works well for site owners and personal assistants. For decades, bots were blocked by default because most were malicious. Personal assistants require a more nuanced approach, and we believe open, verifiable standards will benefit everyone.
How to try it
Ready to hand off your next task? Open Gemini, flip the home-screen toggle from Chat to Task, and tell Gemini what you need done. Starting in the U.S., you can also forward emails to gemini@google.com or text Gemini by following these instructions:
- Open Gemini on Android or iOS and tap Settings
- Tap Channels
- Tap Set up under Text with Gemini
- Verify your phone number
We can’t wait to see what Gemini crosses off your list first.

articles.title: Microsoft AI: Seven new world-class models at scalable price-performance
articles.body:
MAI Licensed Weights: Frontier performance you control
At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability.
But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24/7 doing real engineering work.
That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance.
Here’s the lineup:
Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24/7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost.
Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world-class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools.
MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price.
MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price.
We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.
MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here.
MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry.
MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here.
MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here.
Dragon Copilot Transcribe, built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians.
Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the Artificial Analysis Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol.
We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model.
And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data?
We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th of the cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives.
Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights: models under your control.
Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment.
You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents.
So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale.
And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control.
This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived
articles.body:
More than a decade after Grand Theft Auto V was first released, its sequel is finally launching. On November 19th, GTA VI will be available on both the PS5 and Xbox Series X / S, and it’s quite possibly the most anticipated video game launch of all time.
Part of this has to do with the success of its predecessor, as GTA V sold more than 230 million copies over the last 13 years. Some of it has to do with the sheer length of time between releases, a period that was plagued by leaks and a handful of delays that made the wait even harder for fans.
But GTA VI is now a real thing you can play, and you can also keep track of all of the important post-launch information right here. That includes our own review and interviews with the development team, as well as news on just how the game ends up resonating with players.
- The full GTA VI graphics breakdown on PS5 Pro, PS5, Xbox Series X, and Xbox Series S. We finally have more details about GTA VI’s graphics, including that it’s upscaling 1440p to 4K on base PS5 and Xbox Series X, but PSSR2 on the PS5 Pro. AMD’s FSR Upscaling 4 is used to scale the resolution from 720p to 1080p on Series S. Digital Foundry explains how input lag factored into those choices, as well as the differences between platforms, how well it holds to the target 30fps framerate, plus the impact of VRR.
- Our favorite accessories to level up your gaming setup ahead of GTA VI With Grand Theft Auto VI set to finally launch tomorrow, November 19th, our long-awaited return to Vice City is nearly here. But after all this time, some of the gear you’ve used in San Andreas might feel out of place on the glamorous streets of Leonidas County. Luckily for you, we’ve gathered a few of our favorite Xbox and PlayStation 5 accessories to help your long gaming sessions run as smoothly as possible. The 8BitDo Ultimate 3E — an upgraded pick for Xbox Series X and Series S consoles — is a very capable, comfortable controller with elite-level features, including a high polling rate and adjustable triggers. It’s on the expensive side at $149.99, but the customization and clean execution justify the cost. Read our review. Read Article >
- Today’s Vergecast: GTA VI is the love story of our times. It took 13 years, a reported 10-figure budget, and the weight of the world’s expectations, but Grand Theft Auto VI is here. And it’s fantastic. The Verge’s Andrew Webster takes a break from the game to tell us all about life in Vice City, and why GTA VI’s approach to coffee tells us everything we need to know. Watch | Listen | Get ad-free
- “Our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month.” Lost in the excitement of GTA VI finally launching is the fact that Rockstar employees are in the process of voting on whether or not to unionize. Developer Nestor Uriarte explains the importance of the moment in an essay in The Guardian: Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that. As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more.
- GTA VI is great — and I’m not the only one who thinks so. Now that reviews have dropped for the game, it has skyrocketed to the top of Metacritic’s highest-rated list, surpassing Ocarina of Time (the original, not the remake). Of course, this could change as more reviews trickle in, but for now it’s safe to say that GTA VI was worth the long wait.
- ‘It’s a risk’: How Rockstar built the most detailed (and romantic) GTA yet Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t just the biggest GTA game to date; it’s also the most romantic. Though the series is well known for its sordid assortment of criminal leads, GTA VI switches things up by starring a pair of thieves who also happen to fall in love after meeting while stealing a car. It’s still an open-world action game full of chaos and mayhem. But many players will also be attempting to nurture the budding relationship in between heists. The sprawling game is designed to support both audiences. “It’s a risk,” explains Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North. “It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.” Read Article >
- Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade. That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen. Read Article >
- If you want to play GTA VI on PS5 tonight, download yesterday’s firmware update first. Sony has confirmed the 1.267GB download is mandatory to play the new Grand Theft Auto when it launches at midnight tonight. As with most PlayStation firmware patches, we don’t know what it does though, beyond “some security fixes to the system software.” PlayStation Support US (@PS_Support_US) on X [X (formerly Twitter)]
- GTA VI’s voice actor for Lucia was revealed by… The Game Awards. Rockstar hasn’t publicly said who is playing the two leads in GTA VI, but The Game Awards’ nominee video says that Manni L. Perez has been nominated for Best Performance for her work in the game. GTA VI earned eight nominations, the most of any title, including one for Game of the Year.
- Hacker behind 2022 GTA VI leaks pleads guilty Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other big companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS). Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the company “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS says. Read Article >

articles.title: Software Factory builds 30 complex open source libraries in a month
articles.body:
My software factory builds the kind of software I’d expect a specialist team to spend a long time on, and it keeps that software maintained after it ships. So far that’s a SQLite-compatible database engine, a game engine on deterministic physics, a GPU stack with its own shader compiler, and readers and writers for Word, Excel and PowerPoint files. I run it by myself.
There are 30 libraries in all. 28 reached 1.0 between early October and mid-November, and together they’re nearly 1.9 million lines of handwritten library code. They’ve had 241 releases so far, and 183 of those were on libraries already past 1.0. They’re C# on NuGet, and oneyaml also ships in Rust and Go.
What it built
Documents and the web
OnePdf Complexity Innovation
Read, repair, edit, sign and fill PDFs, and write PDF/A and accessible PDF/UA.
OneDocument Complexity Innovation
Read, edit, recalculate and write Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, and render them to PDF.
OneHtml Complexity Innovation
Parse and edit HTML like a browser, and check pages for accessibility without one.
OneRender Complexity Innovation
Lay out and render HTML and CSS to pixels or tagged PDF, without a browser.
OneFont Complexity Innovation
Load fonts and shape text in any script, with bidi and line breaking.
OneImage Complexity Innovation
Decode, edit, convert and resize images, from PNG and JPEG to layered PSD.
Data and formats
OneLite Complexity Innovation
Embed a SQLite-compatible database that reads and writes the same files as sqlite3.
OneIndex (preview) Complexity Innovation
Run full-text, vector and hybrid search in-process, or in the browser.
OneArchive Complexity Innovation
Compress and unpack zip, 7z, tar and other archives, with the same bytes everywhere.
OneMail Complexity Innovation
Read, write and convert mail stores, Outlook PST included, and send and fetch mail.
OneCrypto (preview) Complexity Innovation
Load keys and certificates, validate certificate paths, and sign and encrypt with OpenPGP.
oneyaml Complexity Innovation
Load, dump and edit YAML in place in Rust, Go and C#, keeping comments.
OneContact Complexity Innovation
Parse and normalize phone numbers, emails, URLs, addresses and names, and find them in pages.
OneDiff Complexity Innovation
Diff and merge text like git, and redline changes between PDFs, digital or scanned.
AI and ML
OneModel Complexity Innovation
Run and train ONNX models in pure C#, on CPU, GPU or in the browser.
OneNlp Complexity Innovation
Tokenize, tag, parse and extract entities from text, and train the models in C#.
OneSpeech Complexity Innovation
Transcribe, time and diarize speech with Whisper and other open models, in .NET.
OneOcr Complexity Innovation
Read text, tables and invoice fields from scans and PDFs.
OneLlm Complexity Innovation
Call Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini models through one API, and run agents as files.
OneModelContext Complexity Innovation
Serve tools to AI agents over MCP, or connect to MCP servers, with OAuth.
Languages, GPU and media
OneEcma Complexity Innovation
Run JavaScript inside .NET under limits, with error reports that explain the failure.
OneShader Complexity Innovation
Compile HLSL to Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU shaders as part of dotnet build.
OneGpu Complexity Innovation
Run compute and ML kernels on Vulkan, Metal or WebGPU from pure C#.
OneAudio Complexity Innovation
Decode, encode, mix and resample audio, measure loudness, and play it on devices.
OneMedia Complexity Innovation
Remux, trim, tag, repair and package video and audio files without re-encoding.
Games and simulation
OneGame Complexity Innovation
Let AI agents build, run, test, inspect and change games through commands, with no editor.
OneMath Complexity Innovation
Compute sin, exp, pow and more correctly rounded, the same bits on every machine.
OnePath Complexity Innovation
Find paths on grids, graphs and navmeshes, build the navmeshes, and steer crowds.
OnePhysics Complexity Innovation
Simulate 2D and 3D rigid bodies, cloth, soft bodies, fluids and vehicles, bit-identical everywhere.
OneScope Complexity Innovation
Scrub, fork and compare runs of a deterministic simulation, recorded or live.
OnePdf implements ISO 32000 for reading, three-step repair of damaged files, the security handler’s revisions 2 through 6, signing, and writing PDF/A, PDF/UA-1 and PDF/UA-2. An outside validator decides whether the output is right: of veraPDF’s own 2,906-file corpus, 2,694 converted to PDF/A-2b and every one of those passed veraPDF. A sweep over GovDocs1, a 5,000-file SafeDocs sample and the veraPDF corpus opened each file and interpreted every page with 0 crashes and 0 hangs. It’s about 120,000 lines of C#.
OnePdf is a from-scratch implementation of ISO 32000 and its PDF/A and PDF/UA profiles. The value is having reading, repair, editing, signing and compliant writing exact in one managed library.
OneDocument covers OOXML, the old binary DOC, XLS and PPT, RTF and ODF, and the Word 6/95 and early Excel layouts come from observed files because there’s no spec for them. A save has to keep every part of the package exactly, including parts the library never touches: over a public corpus of 4,900 files, 111,239 of 111,239 parts came back byte-identical. Real Office judges what it writes, and 718 generated files open in Word, Excel and PowerPoint with no repair prompt. It’s about 285,000 lines of handwritten C#, and it renders through OneRender and the libraries under it.
The formats are existing standards. What it adds is a document model that’s a view over the file’s own markup, so untouched parts go back out as the original zip entries and edits keep unknown elements and extensions in order. The same library renders documents, workbooks and decks to tagged, accessible PDF.
OneHtml implements the WHATWG parser with every insertion mode, Selectors Level 4, the CSS cascade, and the ARIA, AccName and HTML-AAM specs that define the accessibility tree. It’s checked against Chrome itself: across 2,095 pages it matched 1,779,203 of Chrome’s 1,840,086 accessibility nodes. A no-edit round trip is byte-identical on all 18,330 corpus pages and stylesheets. It’s about 85,000 lines of C# on the .NET base library alone.
Edits go through a byte-level source map, so an edit changes only the bytes it touches and old snapshots of the DOM stay valid. It computes the accessibility tree Chromium exposes and runs accessibility checks with no browser, with Chromium’s choices written down as a profile.
OneRender implements CSS from the specs: computed values, the box tree, layout, fragmentation and paged media, painting, DOM events, transitions and animations. Its geometry is checked against Chrome on the same fonts, and its six templates match 3,051 of 3,052 elements at both 1280×800 and 390×844. It’s built on four other factory libraries, OneHtml, OneFont, OneImage and OnePdf, and it’s about 89,000 lines of C#.
It’s a browser-class layout engine packaged as a library, with no JavaScript, networking or clock of its own; the host passes the time. One engine serves both a 200-page report and a game UI that updates every frame, and incremental relayout gives the same result as a full rebuild. Output goes to pixels, a versioned display list a game engine can draw, or tagged PDF/UA.
OneFont implements TrueType, CFF, every GSUB and GPOS lookup type, and the script shapers for Arabic, Indic, the Universal Shaping Engine and Thai/Lao. Indic alone means syllable cutting, reph movement and pre-base matras in Microsoft’s documented feature order. The Unicode 17 conformance files for line, grapheme, word and sentence breaking and bidi pass in full, read unmodified. It’s about 11,500 lines of C# with no dependencies.
OneFont is a from-scratch implementation of OpenType layout and the Unicode text algorithms. The value is having shaping, bidi and segmentation exact in one dependency-free library.
OneImage has its own codecs for PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, TIFF, BMP and ICO, plus ICC v2/v4 color, JPEG 2000 and JBIG2 for PDF images, PSD/PSB layers, metafiles and SVG. On 2,327 JBIG2 streams from government PDFs, 1,925 decode bit-identical to poppler’s pdfimages and the other 402 are its exact inverse, because pdfimages applies the PDF’s decode polarity and OneImage leaves that to the caller. Lossless JPEG 2000 is bit-exact on the T.803 conformance set. It’s about 145,000 lines of C#.
These are existing codecs and formats, written from scratch. The value is having them exact in one managed library, with pixels computed lazily, tile by tile, only when you save.
OneLite reimplements SQLite 3.53.4’s file format, rollback journal, WAL, SQL semantics, result codes and error messages, plus FTS3/4/5, R*Tree and SQLCipher 4 pages. Compatible means it can share a live database with sqlite3: 10,000 interleaved WAL commits stay consistent from both sides. It was written from SQLite’s public docs with sqlite3 as a black box, and differential testing against sqlite3 found 0 unexplained differences in about 12,000 cases. It’s about 115,000 lines of C#.
OneLite is a from-scratch reimplementation of SQLite, and compatibility is the point. The value is a SQLite engine in pure managed code, NativeAOT and the browser included, that reads and writes standard SQLite files.
OneIndex implements known search algorithms: BM25F with block-max WAND, HNSW, rank fusion, UAX #29 segmentation and Snowball stemmers for 34 languages. The stemmers reproduce the published Snowball vocabularies exactly, 11,481,578 of 11,481,578 words. Durability testing ran about 890,000 fault-injection schedules and more than 7,000 process kills with no lost commit. It’s about 70,000 lines of C#.
The algorithms are known ones, implemented from scratch. The value is text, vector and hybrid search exact in one in-process library, which can also serve the same index to a browser as static files.
OneArchive has its own codecs for Zstandard, LZ4, Deflate, Brotli, LZMA and xz, bzip2 and PPMd, and its own readers and writers for zip, tar, 7z, ISO 9660, cab and more. Its compressed output is part of the contract: each codec and level writes the same bytes on every OS, CPU, runtime and thread count, in every 1.x release. PPMd output is byte-identical to what 7-Zip writes. It’s about 95,000 lines of C#.
These are existing codecs and containers, written from scratch. The value is having them in one managed library whose 1.x contract is that each codec and level writes the same bytes on every platform, so the output can serve as a content address.
OneMail implements MIME and Outlook’s formats from Microsoft’s Open Specifications, MSG and PST among them, plus mbox, Maildir, calendars, contacts and SMTP, IMAP and POP3. Untouched MIME writes back byte-identical, 523,424 of 523,424 messages including the Enron maildir. PSTs it writes, including edits made in place to an existing store, open in Outlook. It’s about 112,000 lines of C#.
The formats and protocols are existing ones. What’s uncommon is writing Unicode PST from managed code, as a new file or in place in an existing store, with in-place writes committed by MS-PST’s two-root protocol and the results opened in Outlook. Its forensic recovery got back more items than Outlook’s own repair tool in all 12 damaged stores compared.
OneCrypto implements ASN.1, X.509 and path validation, CMS, PKCS#8 and #12, OpenSSH keys, OpenPGP RFC 9580 with post-quantum algorithms, and the modern curves, all on the .NET base library. OpenPGP messages written by GnuPG, Sequoia, RNP, OpenPGP.js and gosop parse and write back byte for byte, and two-way interop runs against each of them with 0 failures. Path validation passes all 9,572 BetterTLS cases. It’s about 82,000 lines of C#.
OneCrypto is a clean-room implementation of published crypto standards. The value is having them in one managed library that also runs in the browser, with every secret-handling primitive under a timing test.
oneyaml implements one spec, YAML 1.2.2, three times: natively in Rust, Go and C#, at about 87,000, 34,000 and 46,000 lines. The Rust parser scores 402 of 402 on the yaml-test-suite under a strict criterion that also checks its lossless events and exact diagnostics. Every YAML 1.1 behavior is a named setting, off by default.
YAML is an existing standard, and byte-preserving round trips exist elsewhere. What’s uncommon is that typed reads and in-place edits share one parser and one resolver, so they can’t disagree about what a file means, and one shared conformance kit holds the Go and C# libraries to the same cases through their public APIs.
OneContact reproduces libphonenumber 9.0.43’s behavior and implements RFC 5322 email, WHATWG URL, the Public Suffix List and UTS #46. The phone side has 0 mismatches against libphonenumber in 2,819,630 results, and the URL side passes all 896 of WPT’s URL tests. It’s about 50,000 lines of C#.
Each piece reproduces an existing standard or reference library. The value is phones, email, URLs, addresses, names and page extraction exact in one library that never touches the network.
The text core is Myers, patience and histogram diff, held to outside tools: edit lengths equal GNU diff --minimal on 9,483 of 9,483 cases, and three-way merges equal git merge-file byte for byte in all three conflict styles. The document layer marks changes on the PDF pages and re-reads its own marks to confirm they match the change list. It’s about 39,000 lines of C#.
The diff algorithms are known. What it adds is document redlines where every comparison is checked to be invertible: old plus the changes gives new, and new minus the changes gives old. Changes come back typed with resolved values, like “30 days → 60 days”, and a renumbering counts as one change.
OneModel reads ONNX with its own protobuf reader, any opset from 7, and runs it on its own kernels for AVX2, AVX-512, NEON and portable SIMD, with graph optimization, quantization and training. On the ONNX 1.22.0 backend suite it passes 1,580 cases in fast mode with 0 failures. Exact mode has to give the same output hash on every x64 and arm64 path, NativeAOT and the browser, which rules out fused multiply-add and fixes the order of every addition. It’s about 73,000 lines of C#, and its GPU sessions run on OneGpu.
ONNX runtimes exist; OneModel adds an exact mode that gives the same bits on every CPU path and in the browser, at any thread count. The rules are written down, one accumulator per output in a stated order, no fused multiply-add and its own fixed polynomials for exp and tanh, so a port can reproduce the bits. It also trains, in the same managed library.
OneNlp implements five tokenizer families, UAX #29 segmentation, and a full neural pipeline: tagger, lemmatizer, biaffine dependency parser, entity recognizer and classifiers. Its tokenizers match Hugging Face tokenizers and tiktoken with 0 mismatches across 12 families, down to ids, offsets and special-token masks. It’s about 52,000 lines of C#, built on OneModel for inference and training.
The components are established NLP techniques. The value is running and training the whole stack in managed .NET, with models shipped as NuGet packages.
OneSpeech runs existing models: Whisper, Qwen3-ASR, Moonshine and Parakeet for recognition, plus alignment, voice activity detection, diarization and speaker embeddings. It reads PyTorch checkpoints, safetensors and NumPy files itself, and Whisper large-v3-turbo’s word error rate on LibriSpeech is within noise of openai-whisper’s. It’s about 17,000 lines of C#, with the heavy lifting in OneModel and OneAudio.
OneSpeech implements existing published models and decoding methods. The value is running them in managed .NET on OneModel, with no native inference runtime.
OneOcr has its own models, a page detector, line recognizers for Latin, Greek and Cyrillic, and a document extractor, defined by 20 written specs, and it trains them with its own backward passes. Output is bit-identical across AVX-512, AVX2, SSE/NEON and scalar paths at any thread count, which takes a fixed 16-lane accumulation order and its own polynomial exp and tanh. It’s about 43,000 lines of C# on its own SIMD kernels, not OneModel.
When you add an LLM pass, OneOcr sends the page along with its own word list, and the model has to cite the word ids each value came from. Every value is then checked against those words, the rest of the page, or arithmetic over cited amounts, and a value that doesn’t match is marked as a possible hallucination and asked for once more. The check is deterministic, and its spec says a port must reproduce it exactly.
OneLlm puts Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini, first-party and through Bedrock, Vertex and Azure OpenAI, plus any OpenAI-compatible server, behind one message model with streaming, tools, structured output and reasoning replay. Each provider is checked by replaying recorded fixtures that compare request bytes and parsed results. It also has its own prompt template language, diff-tested against Go’s text/template on 12,858,638 generated templates. It’s about 62,000 lines of C#.
The provider layer implements existing vendor APIs. The value is one message model over all of them, with agents, scripts and deciders as files you can persist, fork and resume.
OneModelContext implements every Model Context Protocol revision from 2024-11-05 to 2026-07-28, as client and server, over stdio and Streamable HTTP, with OAuth 2.1 and an embedded authorization server. Run as a black box, it passes the official conformance suite’s server scenarios at every revision. Its JSON-RPC, SSE, HTTP, OAuth and JOSE layers are its own code on the base library, about 43,000 lines of C# in all.
It’s a clean-room implementation of a published protocol. The value is both protocol eras behind one API, so application code is written once against the modern semantics.
OneEcma implements ES2026 in strict and sloppy mode, with its own RegExp engine, ECMA-426 source maps and Intl for six locales. On test262 it passes 22,973 language tests and 18,337 built-ins tests. Error messages and stack traces use V8’s exact wording, and lodash, preact and react SSR output must equal Node’s byte for byte. It’s about 78,000 lines of C#.
The engine is a from-scratch implementation of ECMA-262, 402 and 426. The value is a sandboxed JavaScript runtime in pure .NET whose error reports, built by replaying the failed run with tracing on, say where the failing value came from and how to fix it.
OneShader compiles Shader Model 6 HLSL to three targets, SPIR-V, Metal Shading Language and WGSL, including wave intrinsics, 16- and 64-bit types, bindless resources and cooperative matrices. Every target is checked by outside tools: spirv-val and a GPU run beside DXC’s compile for SPIR-V, naga and browser WebGPU for WGSL, and Apple’s compiler and Metal for MSL. Buffer offsets and strides must equal DXC’s. It’s about 58,000 lines of C#.
It’s an HLSL compiler in C# that runs inside dotnet build: shader mistakes become MSBuild errors on the HLSL line, and the generated C# structs match the compiled layout, so a CPU/GPU layout mismatch fails the build. It also compiles cooperative matrices with bfloat16_t, which the repo states DXC cannot compile.
OneGpu drives Vulkan 1.3, Metal through the Objective-C runtime and browser WebGPU from C#, with no native binaries of its own. Its ML kernels include FlashAttention-style attention that never writes the score matrix to memory and a GEMM that picks cooperative-matrix variants from the device’s capabilities. It’s about 24,000 lines of C# plus HLSL kernels compiled by OneShader.
The kernel algorithms are published ones. What’s uncommon is ONNX-class ML kernels on Vulkan, Metal and browser WebGPU from pure C#, with no CUDA. 41 of its 62 kernel files are written once in HLSL and compile to all three APIs; the rest are vendor fast paths with portable fallbacks.
OneAudio implements Opus, Vorbis, FLAC, MP3, AAC including HE-AAC, and AMR and AMR-WB from the specs, plus BS.1770 loudness. Several have to be bit-exact against the reference: the Opus encoder’s packets match the RFC 6716 reference encoder byte for byte in 269 of 269 configurations, and AMR decoding is bit-exact on all 573 3GPP test sequences. It’s about 57,000 lines of C#.
These are published codecs and loudness standards, written from scratch. The value is having them exact in one managed library, with a mixer that allocates nothing while it renders.
OneMedia reads MP4, Matroska, MPEG-TS, ASF, AVI and a long list of other containers, writes MP4, Matroska, MPEG-TS and WAV, and reads subtitles from SRT to CEA-608 and PGS bitmaps, all without decoding a sample. Tags and facts agree with ExifTool and MediaInfo on 116 files, and 445 untouched tag-edit round trips come back byte-identical. It’s about 134,000 lines of C#.
The container formats are existing standards, implemented from scratch. The value is reading, editing and repairing nearly every common container in one managed library with no dependency beyond the base library.
OneGame is a whole engine: 2D and 3D renderers, client/server sync, its own Noise-protocol encryption, Wayland, X11 and Win32 platform layers, glTF import, and Roslyn generators and analyzers. It’s built on 13 packages from eight other factory libraries plus oneyaml, including physics, GPU, shaders, rendering and audio. Sample games must give the same state hashes on Linux and Windows in CI. It’s about 122,000 lines of handwritten C#.
A game is plain C# and text assets, and every operation is a command that returns JSON: build, run headless, test YAML scenarios, capture frames, record and replay, poke live state over MCP, and hot-reload code into the running game. Determinism rules are compile errors, and the analyzer follows every call out of simulation code to any depth. It’s built so an AI agent can make a game from a terminal.
Correctly rounded means returning the IEEE 754 nearest value of the exact mathematical result, for 21 functions in float and double. OneMath does it with Ziv’s method: a fast table stage settles most inputs, and when the rounding is in doubt a double-double stage and then an exact 500-bit stage run. All 232 float inputs were checked for the 17 unary functions, with 0 not correctly rounded. It’s about 8,500 lines of C#.
Correctly rounded results are the same bits on every machine, which ordinary Math.Sin doesn’t promise: Microsoft’s docs say its result may differ between operating systems or architectures. OneMath never calls Math.Sin or fused multiply-add, an analyzer enforces that, and no 1.x release changes any bit. OnePhysics and OnePath build their determinism on it.
OnePath implements A*, JPS, JPS+, Theta*, HPA*, D* Lite, flow fields, a Recast-class navmesh pipeline and ORCA crowds. Grid path costs equal the Moving AI benchmark’s published optimal lengths, and 3D navmesh coverage is within 0.35% of Recast 1.6.0 on the same settings. Results are bit-identical on x64, arm64 and WebAssembly. It’s about 49,000 lines of C#, built on OneMath.
Results and saved state are bit-identical on x64, arm64 and WebAssembly, so searches, flow fields, navmeshes and crowds restore to the same bytes on every machine in a lockstep or rollback game. The algorithms underneath are known ones, which the repo names, implemented from scratch for grids, graphs, navmeshes and crowds in one package.
OnePhysics covers rigid bodies, joints, ropes, cloth, soft bodies, fracture, particle fluids, shallow water, granular matter, characters, vehicles and ragdolls, in 2D and 3D. All of it has to stay bit-identical, so it uses only exact + - * / and sqrt plus OneMath’s functions, fixed-order reductions and a graph-colored solver. CI hashes every step: 165 of 165 scenarios match on Linux x64 and arm64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64, on eight threads, under NativeAOT and in the browser. It’s about 137,000 lines of C#.
The physics methods are published. What’s uncommon is the guarantee: the same world state, bit for bit, on every OS, CPU, vector width, WebAssembly mode and thread count. That’s what lockstep and rollback multiplayer need, and the tools for it are built in: byte-exact snapshots, per-step hashes, replay checks and a desync finder that reports the first difference.
OneScope’s scope is bounded: its own probe, session and cache formats, and no outside spec. The work is in seek and attach: a seek restores the nearest keyframe and re-simulates to land on the same hash as straight play, and a live attach re-simulates the stream so the viewer’s hash matches the host’s at every step. It’s about 15,000 lines of C#, and the window is built on OneGame.
It treats a deterministic run as a pure function of its recording, so you can seek to any step, fork from it, poke state and see the step where the fork diverges. It attaches to a running program without changing or slowing it, and every window action is also a CLI command and an MCP tool, so an agent can debug with it the same way.
A few up close
OneGame
OneGame is a C# game engine with no editor. A game is plain C# plus text assets. Roslyn source generators write each entity’s change tracking, codecs, deltas and snapshots, and analyzers turn the engine’s rules into compile errors: synced state is fixed-point and only changes through commands, and view code never writes it.
Clients and servers run the same stack, so state syncs between processes with prediction, authority transfer and drift detection. It runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS and the web, and a CLI and an MCP control protocol let an agent build, run, inspect and replay a game from a terminal. It sits directly on nine of the factory’s other libraries.
The repo carries sample games, and CI runs them on Linux and Windows. Solitaire and Lanterns come out with the same state hash on both in every scenario.
OnePhysics
OneGame’s physics comes from OnePhysics, deterministic 2D and 3D physics written from first principles: rigid bodies and joints, ropes, cloth, soft bodies, fracture, particle fluids, shallow water, vehicles and ragdolls, with byte-exact snapshot and restore for rollback netcode.
Determinism is the hard part. Ordinary Math.Sin can return different bits on different platforms, and in a simulation one different bit compounds until the two worlds diverge. So OnePhysics does its math through OneMath, which is correctly rounded and checked against an exact stage on all four billion float inputs. CI hashes the world every step: 165 of 165 scenarios give identical hashes on Linux x64 and arm64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64, under JIT, on eight threads and NativeAOT, and in the browser. In 2D it’s also at or ahead of Box2D.NET on every scene at every thread count.
The GPU stack
OneShader is an HLSL compiler written in C#. It emits SPIR-V for Vulkan, Metal Shading Language and WGSL for WebGPU, and generates the C# bindings for each shader; DXC, spirv-val and naga validate its output in CI.
OneGpu is a pure C# GPU layer over Vulkan 1.3, Metal and browser WebGPU. It used to be part of OneGame. When OneModel, the ONNX runtime, needed the GPU too, I said “Fine, move it to onegpu,” and it became its own library, with ML kernels for GEMM, flash-style attention, convolution and RNNs.
OneModel now runs seven ONNX models on it on an RTX 4070, every row within 1.5× of ONNX Runtime’s WebGPU provider, with the same results on llvmpipe, RADV and an Apple M2 under Metal. OneGpu 1.0, OneModel 1.3 and OneGame 2.0 then shipped in dependency order within about 15 hours.
OneLite
OneLite is a SQLite 3.53.4-compatible database engine in managed C#: the database file format, the rollback journal and WAL, SQL semantics, FTS3/4/5, R*Tree and SQLCipher 4 pages, with an ADO.NET provider and an EF Core adapter.
Compatible here means the files, in both directions. A database the sqlite3 shell wrote reads identically in OneLite, and files OneLite writes pass sqlite3’s integrity_check. The WAL test runs 10,000 interleaved commits between OneLite and live sqlite3 processes on the same database, and it stays consistent from both sides. sqlite3 is a black box to the team; nobody reads SQLite’s source.
SQLite’s own sqllogictest passes all but one of nearly six million records, and on that one SQLite 3.53.4 raises the same integer overflow.
OneDocument
OneDocument reads and writes Word, Excel and PowerPoint in the OOXML formats from a 6,730-page standard, plus RTF and ODF. It also reads the old binary DOC, XLS and PPT, and it comes with a formula engine and rendering to tagged PDF.
The hard part is losing nothing. An OOXML file is a package of parts, and a save has to keep every part exactly, including the ones the library has no reason to touch. OneDocument opened and saved 4,900 real-world files without changes, and all 111,239 of their parts came out byte-identical.
Then real Office judges the output. Desktop Word, Excel and PowerPoint on my laptop open what it writes, all 104 of the authoring and revision documents included, and the formula engine runs against Excel’s own recalculation.
They’re built on each other
21 of the 30 depend on others in the set. The documents side shows it best: OneDocument renders through OneRender, and OneRender is built on four more of the factory’s libraries.
OneDocument’s 1.0 day, Friday, November 6, shows what that means in practice. Three libraries under it shipped what it needed first. OneRender added the tagged-PDF roles OneDocument needed, OnePdf fixed a PDF/UA failure OneDocument found two layers down, and OneImage fixed a crash OneDocument’s fuzzer found.
Anything the agents need from me goes on a projects board on my phone. A request to release is a Ship card: the evidence for the release and a Ship button. All three fixes were on NuGet before OneDocument’s Ship card reached me, and I tapped Ship about ten minutes after it arrived. No team edits another team’s repo; a team that needs something from a library below it asks that library’s team through the project manager.
How the factory runs
Each library starts with a planner agent that designs it through multiple-choice questions, one at a time. A project manager agent answers them for me unless only I can, and every design decision records who made it.
A build lead agent for each library splits the work into units and gives each one to an engineer agent in its own git worktree. Engineers can’t push, tag or publish; the lead checks their work with its own commands and merges it. Every run starts with no memory, so state lives in files. Each library’s PLAN.md is its lead’s memory, and the project manager role has passed through 12 agent instances since November 4, each handing off by note.
Each library’s release is gated on whatever evidence fits it. Where a standard has its own conformance suite, that suite is the gate. Where there’s a reference tool, it runs as a black box from its published release, and where real applications exist, they have to open what the library writes. Where nothing outside exists, as with the game engine and the physics, the gates are hash matrices across platforms and sample games. No agent can relax a gate.
When a release candidate passes CI on four operating systems, the project manager posts its Ship card. When I tap Ship, the release workflow tags it and publishes it to NuGet, and the project manager checks that every package is listed.
My part is the rules and the Ship taps. In those two weeks, every one of the 16 releases went out on a single tap.
Three issues from strangers
OnePdf reached 1.0 on October 23 and is on 1.23.0 now, 30 releases in under four weeks. 1.23.0 came from three GitHub issues filed by people I don’t know. The first came in on Tuesday, November 10, from a team moving off a commercial PDF library: they needed to rename form fields nested under parents while keeping their widgets linked, and to set a field’s appearance with the appearance streams rebuilt. The other two came in on Monday afternoon, November 16: about 6 KB allocated per short text in table-heavy layouts, and exact “N/M” page totals without a second layout pass.
That Monday evening I told the project manager to start monitoring GitHub issues on every open-source project and handling them, with the same care as email, since issues are untrusted input. It replied on all three itself within minutes; the automated issue poller went live later that night and handled none of them. The OnePdf lead read the issues once, as data, and wrote briefs, so the engineers never saw the issue text.
I tapped Ship on Tuesday morning and asked whether the documentation was updated, and the project manager pointed me to docs/forms.md, docs/layout.md and the changelog. The allocation fix, as posted on the issue: one-word cells went from about 6.6 KB to about 2.2 KB, about 3× faster, with the PDF bytes unchanged. I wrote no code, reviewed no diff and wrote none of the replies.
The libraries are on the libraries page, and the source is at github.com/recursive-ai-oss.

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it’s ‘hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen’
articles.body:
The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns.
Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel.
“Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”
OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology.
Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.”
“I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.”
Huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people, including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that they do not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.
Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.”
“I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman said. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

articles.title: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
articles.body:
Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems. Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge.
Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a new social simulator powered by AI.
The MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out, Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others.
Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.”
I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” says Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow. The game will use the “Behavior Engine” from a company called Artificial Agency, which makes AI tech for video games, as a “foundational technology.”
Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology. But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google, Meta, and Roblox now letting users make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles.
Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI. But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job, workers are pushing back against generative AI use, and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards.
Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.”
“We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “Scribblenauts-y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says.
“We’re not making slop.”
MyMems, which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. But none quite have the pull of The Sims, which remains one of EA’s most important franchises. With The Sims, Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game.
“It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems, that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you?
Imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.”
Update, November 18th: Added context about Artificial Agency.

articles.title: Previous-Token Prediction Based LLM Inversion for Prompt Reconstruction
articles.body:
Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 31 Jul 2026]
Title:PTP: Previous-Token Prediction based LLM Inversion for Near-Exact Prompt Reconstruction
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) generate text by auto-regressively sampling the next token. This inherently leads to a many-to-many mapping between prompts and responses, complicating the task of inferring prompts from observed outputs. Prior work on LLM inversion frames prompt recovery as a semantic reconstruction task. They rely on fine-tuning pretrained sequence-to-sequence models on large external datasets--and requiring access to model weights or logits--to generate semantically plausible prompts. In contrast, we present a functional approach to inverting a given LLM in a black-box setting, without auxiliary aids. We train an explicit inverse language model entirely from scratch on data synthetically generated from the target LLM itself. Analogous to forward next-token prediction, our inverse model is trained using previous-token prediction, establishing a generative link between the forward and inverse processes that enables faithful prompt reconstruction. Moreover, it naturally supports diverse prompt reconstructions through sampling, whereby all such prompts induce similar responses under the forward, target LLM. Our approach generalises across datasets and exhibits transferability in reconstructing prompts from responses generated by different LLMs. Further, across the set of token based evaluation metrics for prompt and response reconstructions, our approach outperforms prior work.
