articles.title: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
articles.body:
New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”
The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.
Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”
In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”
Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

articles.title: I had AI read my entire field, Theoretical Astrophysics
articles.body:
I had AI read my entire field.
158,059 papers and 554,670 citations. Every paper with full text screened, 659 of the most important recomputed and checked, and every verified error followed through the papers that cite it. This is the map, and what it says about whether science corrects itself.
Errors that nobody fixed
I spent five years in this field doing my PhD at Caltech, and a few months of that went to errors in the literature that were already known. The equations my code was built on came from Bishop, Gómez, Lehner, Maharaj & Winicour, “High-powered gravitational news” (1997), the paper the subfield's characteristic codes descend from. People knew it had mistakes. The fixes were scattered through some 10,000 lines of intersecting email threads that contradicted each other, and the paper itself was never corrected. The best I could do was correct the record in my own papers: an appendix setting out the full set of equations, made consistent, and a parenthetical “with a sign error in s3 corrected” for anyone reading closely.
That is the limit of human literature review. Mine was not deep: my three thesis papers cite fewer than a hundred papers between them, in a field of tens of thousands. Nobody re-derives every equation they cite, referees check one paper once, and nobody is paid to go back and fix the original. So every student who builds on a broken paper pays the same tax, one at a time, and the correction lives in somebody's inbox. A machine can read the whole field, recompute it, and follow each error to every paper that copied it. So I had one do it. It found errors in my own papers too.
Every dot is a paper
Height is time: the 1960s at the bottom, this year at the top. Each faint line is a citation. The bright dots are the papers everything else leans on, ranked the way Google ranked the early web.
The seed is TAPIR, Caltech's theoretical astrophysics group, where I did my PhD: 4,093 papers by its 326 members since 2004. Add every paper they cite and every paper that cites them and you get 158,059 papers joined by 554,670 citations. The 49,301 drawn here are the ones tied to TAPIR at least three times over.
Watch it grow
The map holds 499 papers from the 1970s, 2,035 from the 1990s and 18,976 from the 2010s. The old layers are the survivors, the papers people working today still cite. Everything else from 1975 has already been forgotten, right or wrong.
Most of what this field knows was written in the last twenty years, by people who are still around to answer email. Hold that thought.
A subfield is a column
Nobody told the layout what numerical relativity is. Papers that cite each other pull together, so a subfield shows up as a column: the same few dozen people writing about the same problem year after year, each layer standing on the last.
There are 32 columns, from fast radio bursts to the Milky Way's halo.
Numerical relativity
Solving Einstein's equations on a computer until two black holes merge. 278 papers in this column, 71 of them TAPIR's, busiest in 2010.
Every subfield has a page: the questions it is organised around and whether each is open, contested or settled, who wrote the central papers and where, how fast it publishes, and which of its errors we traced.
Each open question also carries a flag for what today's AI could do about it. Of 155, a model judged 8 answerable now from data and codes that already exist, 119 ones AI would speed up, and 28 stuck waiting on a telescope or a detector.
Every paper gets screened
Reading a paper carefully costs a few dollars of model time. Screening one costs nothing, so every paper I could get the full text of got screened: 50,269 papers, 421 million words, checked for the fingerprints of the worst kinds of trouble. That covers 76% of the papers drawn here. Nothing before 1991 is on arXiv and journal-only papers aren't open, so the rest got only the checks that run on a database record. (Gold marks TAPIR's own papers.)
- Paper-mill language: none.
- Chatbot residue and hidden instructions to AI reviewers: none.
- Text shared between papers with no author in common: 43 pairs in 34,286 papers, led by successive survey catalogues and data releases. The rest are queued for a human look.
- Retractions: 13 among 184,733 papers with a DOI. None is TAPIR's.
- TODO and FIXME notes shipped to arXiv: 62 papers.
Astrophysics is relatively clean. Whatever is wrong with this literature, it isn't fraud. The one needle that moves is vocabulary: “delve”, “crucial” and friends are 2.5 times as common in 2025 as in 2016.
The 200 that matter get checked line by line
Citations are brutally unequal, and a few hundred papers carry the field. So the 200 most-cited TAPIR papers of 2006–2019 (gold) each got their own AI reviewer with the LaTeX source, tools to run its own calculations, and orders to recompute everything it could: re-derive the equations, test the limits, rebuild the numbers from the paper's own tables. It worked blind, with no access to errata or later papers.
A flag is not a finding. Only what a second reviewer upholds is called an error here.
Thirteen fixed, fifty-six through
About 136 of the 200 were revised between the first preprint and the published paper, so we read those first preprints the same way. 13 verified errors were in the preprint and gone from the journal version, fixed by the referee or by the authors on a second look (purple).
56 went through review and into the journal (gold). On this evidence peer review removes about one error in five. At least two of the thirteen were copied by later papers anyway, from the stale preprint.
A factor of four, 2005–2014
Smith, Kamionkowski & Cooray convert the gravitational waves left over from inflation into an energy density a detector could see. Two factors of one half went missing, so the answer is four times too big: a 6 in the denominator where the textbook has 24. This one was double-checked. The paper's numbers in the paper's formula reproduce its result; the same numbers in the standard formula give a quarter of it.
Watch the years run. Red papers copied the factor of four. The green one said it was wrong, in 2008. The copying carried on until 2014: six copies, one objection.
Five copies for every criticism
Then we cast the net wider. The same recompute-and-verify check, run on 459 more still-cited papers across the map, mostly highly cited ones that a cheaper first read had flagged, upheld 816 more errors. That makes 872 in 433 papers. 159 of them were copied, wrong value and all, into at least one later paper. Counting papers:
367 papers copied an error. 68 criticised one.
Only 47 of the 872 were ever criticised in print, and 21 of those kept being copied afterwards, by 51 more papers. These are floors: we read only the citing papers whose text we hold.
And 872 is a floor for the field too. Only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map got the thorough treatment so far. Scaled up from the papers that did, the likely number of undetected errors in this field's papers cited 100 or more times is about 34,000 (25,000–48,000). How that number is reached →
Half are still being copied 7 years later
How effective is peer review and publishing at detecting and expunging errors from the literature? We can actually measure it.
Share of copied errors still being copied, by years since the paper appeared. Band: 95% interval. 33 errors are old enough to be observed at year 10.
The curve is still at 52% at year 7 and crosses one half at year 8; at year 10 it is at 39%. Counting papers that lean on the affected result without showing which value they used, it crosses at year 9. The errors we traced most thoroughly last longer, crossing at year 10: a shallower search simply finds fewer late copies.
What finally stops an error? Of the 56 errors in the 200 papers read most closely, 52 are still in the latest arXiv version, where a fix is free. Of the 200 papers read most closely, the database records an erratum for 2. And of the 87 errors that did die out, 67 were never criticised by anyone. They faded when the subfield moved on, which retires right answers and wrong ones at the same rate.
4% of the papers that matter, so far
Every paper with open full text was screened and skimmed. The expensive check, the one that recomputes, has reached 659 papers, starting with the most cited. Each bar is the papers on the map with that many citations, filled by how far they have been read.
A field outgrows its errors. It rarely corrects them.
All of this would cost about $2,720 in model time bought at list price, roughly $3 per verified error. In practice it ran within a Claude Max subscription. The whole project, this field and the others, took about 4.9 billion tokens and about 44 hours of my time over 41 days. It is one field, read by a first-generation method, with limits spelled out on the method page. And it is not finished: the deep check has reached only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map, most cited first. The rest of the queue is a budget decision, and so is the next field.
Errors were found by one AI session and re-derived by a second, independent one, and each was confirmed in the version the journal published. Five were also double-checked step by step against the source. No person has checked any of them. As a test, 40 drawn at random went to a third session that saw only the paper and the passage: it found 33 of the 40 wrong, so some named here will not survive scrutiny. If we have your paper wrong, say so and we will fix it and say that we did.

That covers 76% of the papers drawn here. Nothing before 1991 is on arXiv and journal-only papers aren't open, so the rest got only the checks that run on a database record. (Gold marks TAPIR's own papers.)
- Paper-mill language: none.
- Chatbot residue and hidden instructions to AI reviewers: none.
- Text shared between papers with no author in common: 43 pairs in 34,286 papers, led by successive survey catalogues and data releases. The rest are queued for a human look.
- Retractions: 13 among 184,733 papers with a DOI. None is TAPIR's.
- TODO and FIXME notes shipped to arXiv: 62 papers.
Astrophysics is relatively clean. Whatever is wrong with this literature, it isn't fraud. The one needle that moves is vocabulary: “delve”, “crucial” and friends are 2.5 times as common in 2025 as in 2016.
The 200 that matter get checked line by line
Citations are brutally unequal, and a few hundred papers carry the field. So the 200 most-cited TAPIR papers of 2006–2019 (gold) each got their own AI reviewer with the LaTeX source, tools to run its own calculations, and orders to recompute everything it could: re-derive the equations, test the limits, rebuild the numbers from the paper's own tables. It worked blind, with no access to errata or later papers.
A flag is not a finding. Only what a second reviewer upholds is called an error here.
Thirteen fixed, fifty-six through
About 136 of the 200 were revised between the first preprint and the published paper, so we read those first preprints the same way. 13 verified errors were in the preprint and gone from the journal version, fixed by the referee or by the authors on a second look (purple).
56 went through review and into the journal (gold). On this evidence peer review removes about one error in five. At least two of the thirteen were copied by later papers anyway, from the stale preprint.
A factor of four, 2005–2014
Smith, Kamionkowski & Cooray convert the gravitational waves left over from inflation into an energy density a detector could see. Two factors of one half went missing, so the answer is four times too big: a 6 in the denominator where the textbook has 24. This one was double-checked. The paper's numbers in the paper's formula reproduce its result; the same numbers in the standard formula give a quarter of it.
Watch the years run. Red papers copied the factor of four. The green one said it was wrong, in 2008. The copying carried on until 2014: six copies, one objection.
Five copies for every criticism
Then we cast the net wider. The same recompute-and-verify check, run on 459 more still-cited papers across the map, mostly highly cited ones that a cheaper first read had flagged, upheld 816 more errors. That makes 872 in 433 papers. 159 of them were copied, wrong value and all, into at least one later paper. Counting papers:
367 papers copied an error. 68 criticised one.
Only 47 of the 872 were ever criticised in print, and 21 of those kept being copied afterwards, by 51 more papers. These are floors: we read only the citing papers whose text we hold.
And 872 is a floor for the field too. Only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map got the thorough treatment so far. Scaled up from the papers that did, the likely number of undetected errors in this field's papers cited 100 or more times is about 34,000 (25,000–48,000). How that number is reached →
Half are still being copied 7 years later
How effective is peer review and publishing at detecting and expunging errors from the literature? We can actually measure it.
Share of copied errors still being copied, by years since the paper appeared. Band: 95% interval. 33 errors are old enough to be observed at year 10.
The curve is still at 52% at year 7 and crosses one half at year 8; at year 10 it is at 39%. Counting papers that lean on the affected result without showing which value they used, it crosses at year 9. The errors we traced most thoroughly last longer, crossing at year 10: a shallower search simply finds fewer late copies.
What finally stops an error? Of the 56 errors in the 200 papers read most closely, 52 are still in the latest arXiv version, where a fix is free. Of the 200 papers read most closely, the database records an erratum for 2. And of the 87 errors that did die out, 67 were never criticised by anyone. They faded when the subfield moved on, which retires right answers and wrong ones at the same rate.
4% of the papers that matter, so far
Every paper with open full text was screened and skimmed. The expensive check, the one that recomputes, has reached 659 papers, starting with the most cited. Each bar is the papers on the map with that many citations, filled by how far they have been read.
A field outgrows its errors. It rarely corrects them.
All of this would cost about $2,720 in model time bought at list price, roughly $3 per verified error. In practice it ran within a Claude Max subscription. The whole project, this field and the others, took about 4.9 billion tokens and about 44 hours of my time over 41 days. It is one field, read by a first-generation method, with limits spelled out on the method page. And it is not finished: the deep check has reached only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map, most cited first. The rest of the queue is a budget decision, and so is the next field.
Errors were found by one AI session and re-derived by a second, independent one, and each was confirmed in the version the journal published. Five were also double-checked step by step against the source. No person has checked any of them. As a test, 40 drawn at random went to a third session that saw only the paper and the passage: it found 33 of the 40 wrong, so some named here will not survive scrutiny. If we have your paper wrong, say so and we will fix it and say that we did.

articles.title: Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
articles.body:
Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China.
Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
After former CEO Jensen Huang fought for US approval to sell H200 chips in China, Nvidia is now walking away.
“Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.
The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology.

articles.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
articles.body:
Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- American Heart Association
- Summary:
- A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.
- Share:
Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.
The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.
Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.
Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health
The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.
Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.
A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).
However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.
Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.
"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."
FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events
To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.
The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.
Several differences stood out in the analysis:
- Cardiac arrest: Reports involving caffeine and stimulant products were approximately 11 times more likely to mention cardiac arrest than reports involving products without these ingredients.
- Heart attacks: Heart attacks appeared about 4.5 times more frequently in reports associated with energy drinks and stimulant supplements.
- Abnormal heart rhythms: Reports involving stimulant products were roughly four times more likely to include ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal rhythm in the heart's lower pumping chambers) or heart palpitations.
- Other cardiovascular symptoms: The researchers also identified higher reporting frequencies for rapid heart rate (nearly 3 times more often), chest pain (2.71 times more often) and fainting (about 2 times more often).
- Young adults: Approximately 45% of cardiovascular event reports involving caffeine and stimulant products concerned adults between ages 18 and 34.
- Men and women: Comparable patterns appeared in reports submitted for both sexes.
These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.
"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.
Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable
One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.
Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.
How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.
These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.
Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?
Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.
"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."
Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.
Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.
How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports
The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.
Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.
Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).
Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.
The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.
Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.
Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.
Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.

Materials provided by American Heart Association. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella remains confident in Nvidia after Huang’s exit
articles.body:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies.
“It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.
Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report.
While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft.
“I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before [Huang left], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.”
Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO.
“Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill [Gates]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.”

articles.title: The 6 Best Cutting Boards for Anyone Avoiding Plastics
articles.body:
The 6 Best Cutting Boards for Anyone Avoiding Plastics
I didn’t think a sturdy, large cutting board was essential until I put up with a small, flimsy, plastic one for months. When my roommate finally decided enough was enough and grabbed us a huge wooden one, I noticed the difference immediately. I quickly became a member of the “I’m obsessed with my cutting board” club, and discovered that my grandmother is, too: She recently splurged on a titanium cutting board, and says it has completely changed the way she cooks.
These days many people are trying to steer away from plastic cutting boards (shoutout to Quinn Fish for explaining the potentially harmful effects of microplastics in the kitchen). So I decided to poll our team to find out their favorites. Here are some picks that have also transformed everyone’s time chopping, dicing, and slicing in the kitchen.
This titanium cutting board is the exact one my grandmother raves about. The material not only keeps the board hygienic when she uses it for raw meat, but it also makes the board itself super-lightweight (which means it’s easier for her to manage). It’s designed specifically with home cooks in mind, featuring a knife sharpener, handle, and grinding area.
Something to keep in mind is that Titanium (or any metal) can actually dull your knives faster than wood or plastic. If sharpening your knives more frequently is something you’re worried about, then you might want to consider another material.
Gorilla Grip’s stainless steel cutting board has quickly become Deputy Food Editor Kristina Razon’s go-to when cooking. She loves how the rubber edges keep it from slipping while she’s chopping, and the stainless steel material makes it odor- and stain-resistant “which is ideal for prepping raw or cooked meat, fish, or really anything that tends to leave residue,” she explains. Just note: The same disclaimer about sharpening knives from the board above rings true here as well.
Jill Waldbieser has been using these boards for five years and says they still look brand-new. “They are self-healing, dishwasher-safe, and roll up so you can slice and chop on them, then curl them up and dump the contents into a hot pot or pan with zero issues,” she says.
This 100% plant-based cutting board is a recent favorite of Shopping Writer Micki Wagner. She had high hopes when testing the board, and it did not disappoint. It’s large enough to chop multiple things at once, super durable so there aren’t knife marks, and dishwasher-safe for easy cleanup.
Micki also loves this small cutting board, which quickly became her go-to for pretty much everything except major jobs (read: when a ton of chopping is required). It may look made of wood, but it’s actually paper composite, and its non-slip grips make it dependable for whatever she’s slicing.
Social Media Manager Andrea Kaufman had been wanting to upgrade from her plastic cutting boards for a while, but was worried a wooden one might have the same intimidating maintenance requirements as a cast iron skillet. Her new Hexclad board hasn’t been hard to maintain (so far). It’s super-sturdy, and the built-in handles and grooves on the sides are nice touches, so it’s easy to carry and can tackle cutting meat (actually the first thing she used it for). “I haven’t used it for entertaining yet,” she says, “but I definitely plan to!”
Do you have a favorite plastic-free cutting board? Tell us about it in the comments!

articles.title: More banks says customers using AI agents are on their own — even if they get hacked
articles.body:
Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked.
AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.
But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.
“As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.”
JPMorgan and Bank of America, the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eighth largest bank, changed its terms today.
Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch.
As AI startups look for more revenue, breaking into personal finance presents an attractive opportunity for companies to add value for customers and wet their beaks in the stream of fees generated by the sector. But if consumers are already leery of sharing their email or chat records with an AI agent, bank and brokerage accounts offer a new trust challenge.
Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”
Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat. Markets shuddered briefly in reaction to the prospect of AI tools making it easier for consumers to avoid unnecessary fees or low-interest deposit accounts that pad bank margins. But if AI agents become an important way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway. Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability.
The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service, and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off.

articles.title: Nvidia created a weird bit of intrigue by not filing a routine SEC report
articles.body:
During Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She said Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why.
The delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it, economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results.
The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items.
The announcement of the delay was so unusual that UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked about it after the public earnings call. Nvidia told him the delay was related to whether the company would need to disclose additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang in the 10-Q.
“The company announced that the 10-Q will be filed ‘in the coming weeks’ – later than usual. When queried on our callback, management indicated this was related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing,” Arcuri wrote in his research note. (Arcuri still rates the stock a “buy” by the way, although he did lower his price target to $220 from $240. The stock is now trading around $150).
Notably, on the same day that Nvidia reported earnings, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors.
So the mystery thickens: What will Nvidia disclose? We’ll have to wait and see. (Nvidia has not yet responded to our request for comment.)
The delay suggests the company may have more to say about its mounting legal troubles. Nvidia is now facing multiple federal investigations over allegations that its partners were selling restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. So far, the scrutiny has come from a number of congressional committees; the Department of Justice looking into Megaspeed, the company run by a woman with whom Huang had an affair and who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy; and now, reportedly, the SEC.
Additionally, Nvidia is conducting its own internal investigation into Huang after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang (the Megaspeed executive), and allegations surfaced that he also had affairs with other Nvidia employees.
There’s little doubt that Wall Street will scrutinize that 10-Q once it’s finally filed. The intrigue brings to mind the old saying: “Doctors bury their mistakes. Lawyers put theirs in prison. And accountants hide theirs in the footnotes.”

articles.title: Cambridge Dictionary Names 'Human' Its 2026 Word of the Year
articles.body:
Cambridge Dictionary Names 'Human' Its 2026 Word of the Year 18
			
		 	
				Cambridge Dictionary has named "human" its 2026 Word of the Year, reflecting growing concerns about artificial intelligence and its impact on what it means to be human. "AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. "Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children." The Associated Press reports:  The adjective derived from the Latin "humanus" and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as "having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines." [...] Other word contenders for 2026 included "agent," for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and "analogue" for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology.

articles.title: Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now
articles.body:
Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now (theverge.com) 52
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Verge: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he's AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. "I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy's organization around AGI?" he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn't think frontier models like Claude are conscious. "I don't think so," he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman's view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic's team has "wireheaded" themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn't quite as firm about it. "It's a good debate," he said. "I'm not sort of dogmatic about it. What I'm saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?"
I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter's questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us." "Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be," he said. "But remember, the model has no limits. It'll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it."
Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. "If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?" he asked. "If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That's the debate." "I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one -- at least in a democracy -- can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there's only capital and there's no labor. I mean, I don't know, that's not an economy." "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic."

articles.title: What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
articles.body:
If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.
Nvidia’s rise, visualized
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat.
Nvidia’s rise, visualized
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat.
It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?
But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.
It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.
If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.
TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.
Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.
Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.
Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?
But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.
And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.
Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.
But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.
In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.
On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.
Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.
“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”
Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.
In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.
Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

articles.title: Our favorite accessories to level up your gaming setup ahead of GTA VI
articles.body:
With Grand Theft Auto VI set to finally launch tomorrow, November 19th, our long-awaited return to Vice City is nearly here. But after all this time, some of the gear you’ve used in San Andreas might feel out of place on the glamorous streets of Leonidas County. Luckily for you, we’ve gathered a few of our favorite Xbox and PlayStation 5 accessories to help your long gaming sessions run as smoothly as possible.
Our favorite accessories to level up your gaming setup ahead of GTA VI
Looking for a headset or a pro-grade controller for your return to Vice City? We have some recs.
Controllers
The 8BitDo Ultimate 3E — an upgraded pick for Xbox Series X and Series S consoles — is a very capable, comfortable controller with elite-level features, including a high polling rate and adjustable triggers. It’s on the expensive side at $149.99, but the customization and clean execution justify the cost. Read our review.
PlayStation 5 owners looking for a controller upgrade, meanwhile, might consider the DualSense Edge, Sony’s first-party pro-style controller. In addition to a variety of extra function buttons and paddles, the wireless gamepad sports adjustable trigger heights and swappable joysticks (in case the potentiometers start to drift). It’s a little bit heavier than Sony’s regular DualSense, and the battery life isn’t quite as good, but it offers customization you won’t find on the console’s default controller. Read our review.
Sony DualSense Edge
Sony’s pro-style controller, the DualSense Edge, might suffer from shorter battery life than the standard DualSense model, but it features great software integration with the PlayStation 5 and plenty of customizable components.
Charging docks
Nothing’s worse than having to pause a heist so you can go hunt down a fresh set of AA batteries. The PowerA Duo Charging Station includes a rechargeable battery and replacement rear doors for two Xbox Series X / S or Xbox One controllers. Simply set them on the dock, and they’ll start charging.
PowerA’s PlayStation equivalent charges two DualSense Wireless Controllers simultaneously, with an included AC adapter, and comes with a two-year warranty.
TVs
The 2026 Roku Pro Series is the brand’s first OLED, and the 55-inch version retails for $999.99, which is on the low end of the price spectrum for OLED. Games feel richer and more immersive on OLED panels, thanks to their deeper black levels, which are the result of unlit pixels or sections of the screen. Each Pro Series panel also sports a 120Hz refresh rate, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and both low latency and variable refresh rates for gaming.
For a more premium offering, the Sony Bravia 8 II is one of our favorite screens for movies, with an engaging, immersive picture and excellent image processing. It has great gaming features, too, like a 120Hz refresh rate with variable refresh and an automatic low-latency mode. It’s not cheap, but the OLED makes for an excellent upgrade to your setup. Read our review.
Headsets
Sony’s latest first-party headset, the $99 PlayStation Pulse Wireless, launches the same day as GTA VI. My colleague Cameron Faulkner recently went hands-on with the wireless headset ahead of its launch on November 19th, and came away impressed with its overall audio quality and comfort. The newest Pulse is also straightforward to set up and use, especially when paired with devices like the PlayStation Portal that support PlayStation Link, Sony’s proprietary low-latency audio connection. It also offers Bluetooth for use with other devices.
For Xbox gamers, it’s hard to beat the SteelSeries Arctis Nova 3X, which retails in multiple colors for $109.99 or less. The wireless headset is lightweight, comfortable, and compatible with a wide variety of other consoles and mobile devices as well, for those rare moments when you aren’t playing GTA VI.
If you’d rather the simplicity of a wired option, Sony’s InZone H6 Air skips the batteries and dongles, instead opting to plug straight into your controller. This open-back gaming headset is lightweight and comfortable, which is great for long hours and late nights. My colleague Cameron Faulkner described its sound as “spectacular,” with several equalizer options available for helping fine-tune the sound to your liking. Read our review.
One additional upgrade
Ikea’s Poäng chair balances affordability and comfort, with wide, supportive armrests that are just the right height for holding a controller. It comes in a variety of frame materials and cushion colors, too, making it easy to match your other furniture or console. This is my personal chair for console gaming, and I recently added a matching ottoman to the set for maximum relaxation.

articles.title: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
articles.body:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime (
https://maritime.sh
). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents.
Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY
There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is:
You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins.
It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem.
We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction:
1. Agent lifecycle management.
There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime.
There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up.
2. Custom environments.
Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies.
Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely.
3. Cost optimization.
If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure.
So what did we build differently?
We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents.
We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency.
As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed.
Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research.
We want your feedback.
If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build.
Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing?
Happy to answer any questions in the comments.
https://maritime.sh

articles.title: 'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64
articles.body:
'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64 (calif.io) 18
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader HnT writes: Security researchers at Calif have disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2-rated memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. By sending a malformed string ending in a stray = character, attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write to leak sensitive memory or achieve pre-auth remote code execution on major platforms like Jira, Jenkins, and Keycloak. Although Calif says the vulnerability is difficult to exploit, Oracle released a critical patch update Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to update immediately. OpenJDK's security advisory can be found here.
The Calif researchers warned that vulnerable systems could remain exposed for five to 10 years, given how slowly some organizations patch their infrastructure.

articles.title: Hand-Marbled Papers Ground Sylvain Lefebvre’s Surreal Landscapes
articles.body:
Hand-Marbled Papers Ground Sylvain Lefebvre’s Surreal Landscapes
Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of Sylvain Lefebvre. A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.”
The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux. Collaged, hand-marbled papers beneath the delicate layers of oil paint represent the barely visible or unknown. And trees group closely in the background darken in the distance, while diminutive figures climb around and relax at the base of monumental trunks.
Summer 2026 marked France’s hottest ever documented since records began, during which rainfall was low and unprecedented wildfires raged. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, where the effects of the climate crisis are dramatic and impossible to ignore. In Journeys Into the Unseen Forest, Lefebvre delves into an imaginary realm where humans coexist harmoniously with flora and fauna, and old-growth sentinels harbor a wide range of life.
The artist says, “I wanted to put myself in the place of a forest and its trees by asking myself the following question: How is it that when we look at nature, whatever form it takes, it always appears balanced, while the trees that make it up can grow in such unbalanced ways… twisted, diagonally or horizontally, struggling to find their way towards the light?”
In “The Quercus Corallium,” a white tree glows like a sacred spirit, and in “The Polyphane Pachidermus,” one can imagine the canopy extending forever into the blue distance. “In the unseen forest, [Lefebvre] discovers species of trees that have never been seen before,” the gallery says. “They are completely plausible species that may exist somewhere in the few corners of the world that have not yet been discovered. Perhaps they are trees of the future.”
Journey Into the Unseen Forest continues through December 23 in London. See more on Lefebvre’s Instagram.

articles.title: The first Nvidia RTX Spark mini PCs launch today from Asus, Dell, and MSI
articles.body:
After the first RTX Spark laptops launched earlier this year, Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X chip is also now available in desktops from Asus, Dell, and MSI. More RTX Spark desktops are coming later from Acer, Gigabyte, and HP, while Microsoft’s Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is slated to start shipping this month. The new mini PCs include a 6144-core Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU, 20-core Nvidia Grace CPU, and up to 128GB of memory. That high-end hardware comes with a price to match — Asus’s ProArt GR1X starts at $4,499 for a configuration with 64GB of memory and 1TB of storage.
The first Nvidia RTX Spark mini PCs launch today from Asus, Dell, and MSI
These desktop PCs can pair Nvidia’s ‘superchip’ with up to 128GB of memory for running local AI models.
Like the RTX Spark laptops that compete with the MacBook Pro and the DGX Spark desktop Nvidia launched last year, the new mini PCs are Mac Mini or Mac Studio alternatives for developers working with local AI models, as well as RTX-accelerated software. That includes the AI-powered features for tools like Adobe Premiere and Photoshop, and new DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support in Blender 5.3.
They can run games too, and Windows on Arm game support is improving, but at these prices, that’s not a realistic reason to pick one up yet. Nvidia says they can act as a “dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents,” and deliver “up to 1 petaflop of AI performance.” They also feature native CUDA support and access to Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux.

articles.title: Waymo Robotaxis Pulled From Freeways Indefinitely
articles.body:
Waymo Robotaxis Pulled From Freeways Indefinitely (arstechnica.com) 46
			
		 	
				Waymo has temporarily suspended freeway operations across all its robotaxi markets after California regulators ordered the company off the state's highways over repeated incidents involving construction zones. The restriction follows a June recall (PDF) of nearly 3,800 vehicles and subsequent software updates (PDF) that failed to prevent further incidents, including a robotaxi driving past a California Highway Patrol rolling roadblock. Ars Technica reports:  "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," Waymo told Ars. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations."
Waymo also told Ars it was continuing to work with the various California agencies that regulate transport. Until the suspension, Waymo was only conducting highway operations in Los Angeles and the Bay Area in California, as well as in Arizona.

articles.title: Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page
articles.body:
Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page
As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits, the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil. The new direction took him somewhat by surprise, as he realized one day he had been focusing much more on fauna than he had in years past.
“I think it has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings,” Cian tells Colossal. He felt compelled to get closer to what he describes as elemental raw matter, generated through eons of mysterious and fascinating evolutionary processes. “I think that’s what it comes down to: drawing something that hasn’t itself been designed by someone else.”
Cian’s technical aptitude is obvious, but for him, a work isn’t truly complete unless there’s another kind of investment. “For me, achieving a result I’m truly satisfied with is a considerable challenge because my approach is emotional long before it is descriptive,” he says. Truly understanding and sympathizing with a creature propels the process.
Light also plays an integral role in his deceptively simple monochrome approach: Cian highlights whatever the light touches and leaves everything else alone. A piece feels finished when “areas that remain black stop feeling black,” he says, balancing perception and technicality in equal measure.
The artist spends hours researching a subject before rendering it on paper, watching documentaries and browsing publications that give him a sense of their habitats and behaviors, but he resists working from printed images. Even the textures that, from a distance, may look realistic, are actually intuitive and imagined. “I never copy photographs,” Cian says. “I study the anatomy and then reconstruct it, sometimes exaggerating certain features, in a pose that allows me to feel as though I’m in the presence of that particular creature.”
See more on the artist’s Instagram.

articles.title: This Is the Perfect Gift for Every Kind of Cook (at Every Price Point!)
articles.body:
This Is the Perfect Gift for Every Kind of Cook (at Every Price Point!)
Some gifts are unwrapped, enjoyed for a season, and tucked away. Others immediately become woven into how life is lived for decades: the Dutch oven pulled out for slow-simmered Sunday suppers, the fluted pie dish brought to the table for milestone birthdays, or the stovetop kettle whistling in sync with quiet morning rituals.
Made for making since 1925, Le Creuset has spent a century creating cookware for those who find genuine joy in the kitchen. Every enameled cast-iron vessel, sturdy stoneware dish, and refined accessory is crafted with intention: made to last, built to be shared, and designed to anchor the moments that stay with us long after we clear the table. Whether you’re shopping for a dedicated home baker, an outdoor grill enthusiast, or a passionate host who turns dinner into an event, Le Creuset pieces are thoughtfully made to give and cherish for a lifetime.
To help you make a lasting impression this season, here’s the ultimate Le Creuset gift guide for every price point to inspire new kitchen traditions for generations to come.
For the Chef
Serious home cooks rely on resilient, high-performance cookware that can pivot effortlessly from blazing stove burners to low-and-slow oven braises. These durable staples will quickly become the pieces they reach for every day.
Under $50: Every great home chef knows that a calm, inspired cooking flow starts with smart mise en place. Sized perfectly for measuring spices, herbs, and minced garlic, the Vancouver Pinch Bowls Set helps every recipe shine. Glazed with Le Creuset’s scratch- and stain-resistant enamel, they’re thoughtful and functional for any culinary enthusiast.
Under $150: Crafted with a responsive aluminum core sandwiched between layers of gleaming stainless steel, the Signature Stainless Steel Fry Pan delivers flash-searing heat with surgical precision. It’s an essential tool for reducing pan sauces, browning proteins, and perfecting delicate omelets without sticking.
Under $350: With shallow sides and a broad base, the 3.5 qt Signature Round Wide Oven is a workhorse for searing large batches of meat in a single layer before gently braising them to fork-tenderness. It’s an essential kitchen centerpiece that makes every meal memorable.
For the Baker
Baking is an act of love grounded in patience, precision, and dependable techniques. These heirloom-worthy stoneware and cast-iron essentials are made to make every recipe shine, helping your favorite baker create patisserie-level showstoppers.
Under $50: A charming festive detail with a real culinary purpose. Crafted from dense stoneware, the Christmas Tree Pie Vent releases steam from bubbling fruit pies during baking, eliminating soggy bottom crusts and boil-overs. It’s a joyful, practical stocking stuffer that spreads cheer with every bake.
Under $150: Inspired by a century of artisanal craftsmanship, the versatile Heritage 3-Piece Rectangular Baking Dish Set nesting trio is the ultimate foundation for sweet and savory holiday staples. Crafted from durable stoneware that distributes heat evenly without burning delicate edges, it effortlessly transitions from baking bubbly cinnamon rolls, berry crisps, and gratins in the oven straight to a festive table spread.
Under $350: The Signature Oval Bread Oven is the ultimate showstopper for the artisan breadmaker. Designed specifically for bâtards, sandwich breads, and longer sourdough or artisan loaves, its domed enameled cast-iron lid traps steam to yield maximum rise, an open crumb, and a crisp, crackling crust every time.
For the Grill Master
Cooking over an open flame calls for cookware with rugged construction that thrives under intense heat. Give the outdoor enthusiast gear engineered to handle fire grates, charcoal grills, and smokers with uncompromising culinary control. (Even if they’re just making dinner on the patio.)
Under $50: Built specifically to withstand the searing temperatures of live-fire cooking, the heavy-duty Outdoor Slotted Turner is made to last through season after season at the grates. It’s a professional-grade outdoor staple that will make a lasting impression on any backyard barbecuer. (It also has a built-in bottle opener on the handle, which we think is extraordinarily clever.)
Under $150: A solid Butcher Block is one of those clever gifts they didn’t know they needed. Upgrade their plastic cutting board with a thick, knife-friendly hardwood surface that can handle slicing whole smoked briskets, carving turkeys, or breaking down roasted cuts.
Under $350: If we could gift one thing to a grill master, it would be the Alpine Outdoor Collection Rectangular Griddle designed specifically for the intense demands of outdoor gas grills, charcoal embers, and campfire cooking. Its durable matte black enamel coating requires no seasoning, making it easy to sear delicate fish, fire-charred vegetables, and sizzling morning bacon in the open air.
For the Host
For those who love to bring people together, cooking is all about connection, atmosphere, and the joy of welcoming friends around the table. These versatile, presentation-forward pieces bridge the gap between oven and dining room, making hospitality feel effortless. They may even put your gift to immediate use!
Under $50: Topped with an elegant gold star knob, the Noël Collection Mini Cocotte brings instant magic to group gatherings. Use it for baking individual French onion soups, serving baked dips, or delighting guests with personal lava cakes at their place settings.
Under $150: Substantial and generously scaled, this glazed stoneware Serving Platter features elevated rim detailing to keep savory pan juices and dressings contained. It turns holiday roasts, grilled skewers, and colorful antipasti boards into an undeniable visual feast.
Under $350: The centerpiece for lively winter gatherings, the enameled cast-iron Alpine Signature Fondue Set is made to make new traditions. It maintains gentle, even warmth for molten Gruyère or rich chocolate fondues, inviting family and friends to linger, dip, and connect long after dinner is served.
Bonus Favorites
If you want to present an iconic, enduring masterpiece that becomes part of a home’s story forever, look no further than Le Creuset’s legendary enameled cast iron Dutch ovens. The elongated design of the Traditional Oval Dutch Oven easily accommodates whole chickens, pork loins, and long roasts with room to spare.
For a festive heritage piece you’ll look forward to using every year, the Noël Collection Holiday Tree Signature Round Dutch Oven is an intricate seasonal heirloom embossed with evergreen motifs and crowned with a gleaming gold star knob. And last but certainly not least, the 5.5 qt Signature Round Dutch Oven is the undisputed icon of the culinary world. It’s sized to feed families, celebrate holidays, and simmer memories for a lifetime of shared meals.

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
articles.body:
After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, “very, very far.” The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet — equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours.
NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
It’s taken Voyager 1 almost 50 years to journey farther from Earth than light can travel in 24 hours.
It’s the farthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1’s journey isn’t over yet. It’s been heading toward a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. That star is 17 light-years away, meaning Voyager 1 won’t pass by it for around 40,000 years, despite traveling at nearly 38,000 mph.
The light-day milestone is a remarkable feat alone, but especially so when you consider that Voyager 1 is still operational. NASA has done well to keep it functioning, and it can continue to send back readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields, and space-bound particles, though it now takes radio signals an entire day to travel between Earth and the spacecraft. Voyager 2, which launched 16 days before its twin, is also expected to reach a distance of 1 light-day away from Earth, but not until 2035.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype
articles.body:
How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade.
Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype
Thirteen years later, Rockstar has crafted a worthy successor to GTA V and the new standard-bearer for open-world games.
That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen.
Even more remarkable? The game was actually worth the wait.
At this point I’ve spent nearly 80 hours in Leonida, GTA VI’s fictional take on Florida. And what I’ve experienced is a game that combines the wide-open freedom offered in GTA V with the remarkable level of immersion from the studio’s 2018 release Red Dead Redemption 2, while also improving on both qualities. At the same time, it’s also the most mature GTA game Rockstar has ever made, merging the criminal antics and absurdist humor the series is known for with a love story that gives you new ways to interact with the world and new reasons for wanting to push forward. This is the GTA game the studio has been building toward for its entire existence.
Let’s start with that new premise. GTA V introduced the idea of multiple protagonists to the series, and VI takes that concept in a different direction.
