It’s a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story about Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, two small-time criminals who meet while, of course, stealing a car. It’s the most GTA-possible meet-cute. The idea is that you can play as both characters individually and also build their relationship over the course of the game. Things start out relatively slow. At the outset, Lucia is in prison, and you play solely as Jason, getting things ready for when she gets out. You can fix up your ramshackle house — that involves actually nailing down new stairs and rolling out paint on the walls — and also start building up a nest egg through means that are not exactly legal.
Jason and Lucia’s relationship grows naturally over the course of the game, but it’s also a slow buildup to becoming the inseparable pair they were by the end of my playthrough. GTA VI approaches most of the experience with confident and deliberate pacing. Even when you control them individually, the characters are often together, either just hanging out or partnering for a crime. And being able to play as both is one of the game’s standout features. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. Before that, you play as both leads mostly solo, learning who they are as people, before you’re given free rein to switch between the two.
What’s great about the premise is how seamlessly it fits with what you’re actually doing in the game. There’s some bigger-picture stuff that I won’t spoil, but generally speaking, the main goal in GTA VI is to make a lot of money so that Jason and Lucia can get out of the criminal life for good and retire somewhere comfortably. And outside of the big story missions, you’re largely free to choose how you go about that. You can rob jewelry stores, steal cars, raid drug dens, or even search for hidden treasure at the bottom of the sea. Over the course of the game you’ll also meet different criminals who serve as fences, so you can sell them whatever you’ve got to build up your savings account. Sometimes they’ll even text you targets that are particularly lucrative.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play. I’m not a big fan of armed robbery, for instance. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. But I love getaway chases, and so stealing cars became my main form of income. Most importantly, though, this structure gives you a lot of reasons to go out in the world and explore. The missions take you all over the map — which is actually entirely accessible from the very beginning, if you choose to play that way — including not only the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City, but also tourist beaches, swamps, trailer parks, and a wild variety of other locations, each with its own landscape to explore and characters to meet.
To be clear: Despite being larger, more mature, and more lifelike, this is still very much GTA. This is a game about chaos and crime. This comes across in a few ways. First, there are those smaller missions where you never really know how things will play out. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. The world itself is full of unpredictable moments that force you to think on your feet. Several times I stopped my car to talk to an NPC whose vehicle broke down on the side of the road. In one instance the driver just swore at me to leave her alone. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. I delivered her packages and ended up dealing with everything from porch pirates to tigers.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play.
There are also the multistep heists, which return from GTA V more intricate and complex. These are the big scores and involve several different missions: You spend time getting the right gear and gathering all of the information you need to actually pull them off. Even some of the sub-missions can be gigantic, including one where you have to go undercover for weeks of in-game time to get everything you need in order. But the payoff is incredible. The heists play out like over-the-top action set-pieces, as if they were pulled out of a Christopher Nolan movie like Tenet or Inception (but without all of the sci-fi twists). Even better, all of the missions in the game feel streamlined with a new checkpoint system that allows you to spend less time replaying sequences after failing, and if you fail too many times, you can just skip that mission altogether. There are still a few too many prolonged shootouts, but the checkpoints mean they’re much less tedious than in past GTA games.
All of this action is crammed into a world that isn’t just huge, but also feels more alive than ever before. Like in Red Dead Redemption 2, you can talk with any NPC, but here you have more options, letting you either greet them or, if you feel like causing trouble, taunt them. Most of the time you’ll get a simple “hey” or someone begging for a few dollars. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. The owner of the shop called the cops, and so I figured if I was in this much trouble, I might as well empty the register. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops.
Another important thing to note: While the game retains the series’ satirical tone in many ways, the humor doesn’t punch down like in past GTAs, at least from what I’ve played. Instead it makes fun of stuff that deserves to be made fun of: men’s rights activists, NFT bros, conspiracy theorists, Bryan Johnson.
But what really makes the world so special are all the small, meaningful details. Changing your clothes is a lot of fun, but it also helps keep the cops off your back when you’re wanted. Eating and drinking helps improve your physical abilities. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. That includes taking the bus, which runs on a predetermined route, making stops along the way. You can rent electric scooters, and just like in real life, they’re a menace clogging up the streets of Vice City. Your cars even need to be gassed up from time to time.
It’s a careful balancing act. These details make the world feel more nuanced and textured, but they’re also minor enough that they don’t feel tedious. This isn’t The Sims where you’re constantly monitoring your characters’ bodily functions. Usually, I only remembered to eat when the fitness app on my phone told me I needed more protein, and I didn’t once have a car break down because I forgot to fill up the tank. These smaller mechanisms are just enough to add a sense of realism without getting in the way of the action. You can also ignore a lot of them; at no point do you need to shower, but you might hear some snide remarks from your partner if you don’t.
Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Crime bosses might text you a location to meet up, for instance, and you can add it to your GPS and head over. Or Lucia might text Jason a link to a funny video, which you can then open in a social networking app, and you can even read the comments. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive.
Despite spending more than 70 hours in the world, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience
I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. When the two are together, you can press one of the shoulder buttons to make them hold hands. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. At first I used this strategically, imagining that if a couple holding hands was casing a jewelry store, it would be much less conspicuous. But eventually, as I grew to know the couple, it just became a thing I did without thinking about it. These two are crazy in love; of course they’re going to hold hands all the time. You can even do little things like make a coffee and choose to hand it to your partner instead of drinking it yourself, and all of these acts improve your relationship, which in turn impacts how the characters relate to each other and how some of the narrative elements play out.
You don’t have to do any of that. There are just so many ways to interact with the world that different players will find their own things to fixate on. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. I barely touched on any of those elements and still felt like I had a substantial experience.
Jason and Lucia are two very different people, each with their own kinds of stories to explore within the game. The big missions are cinematic heists that usually involve some combination of the two. But there are large, branching narratives that are only playable as one or the other character. Jason, for instance, has an old friend who is trying to start a record label in the back room of a strip club. As with the best GTA stories, the tale steadily escalates until you’re feuding with a famous rapper and facing down a number of life-or-death situations. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. These storylines are so big and absorbing that I would often forget about the main campaign for long periods of time.
It’s not that there are zero issues with the game. The combat is still clunky, and the weapon wheel is still frustrating; there were multiple times when I accidentally equipped a flashlight instead of a shotgun when in the heat of battle. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine.
Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. There have been great examples of the form since then — Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Control Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077 (eventually) — but none that approach the scale and detail of Rockstar’s works. Certainly none that attempted to do it in anything like the contemporary, real-world setting that has made GTA so pervasive. Now that mantle has been passed to GTA VI.
To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. The most pretentious indie game of 2026? It exists in GTA VI.
For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA VI is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it.
Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

articles.title: FailTrace – Reproduce a failed GitHub Actions run locally from its URL
articles.body:
Stop guessing why CI failed. Reproduce it locally.
Paste a failed GitHub Actions run URL. FailTrace finds the job and step that failed, matches them to the workflow file at that exact commit, pulls the failure out of the logs, and tells you what stands between you and reproducing it on your machine.
failtrace inspect https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/123456789   # why did it fail?
failtrace plan    https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/123456789   # how would it be reproduced?
failtrace repro   https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/123456789   # reproduce it in Docker
Status: early development. All three commands work. repro covers Linux jobs whose failing step is
a run: script. See the roadmap and limitations.
act runs your workflows locally, and it's great at that. FailTrace
answers a different question: why did this particular run fail, and can I make it fail the same way here?
- It starts from a failed run, not a workflow file. You get the exact commit, attempt, job, matrix combination, and failing step. Nothing to configure.
- It focuses on the failure. The goal is to replay only what the failing step needs, not the whole workflow.
- It gives you a verdict. You get a diagnosis now. Later you'll also get reproduced / not reproduced / flaky, plus what differed between CI and your machine.
Real output for a failed prometheus/prometheus run (trimmed):
✗ CI · prometheus/prometheus
  "remote/otlp: remove delta-to-cumulative conversion"
  pull_request · on codex/remove-otlp-deltatocumulative · @ cf7d324 · attempt 1 · failure
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
✗ Job: Go tests  (failure)
  Runner     ubuntu-latest → ubuntu-26.04 (20261116.202.1) · runner 2.338.2
  Workflow   .github/workflows/ci.yml → jobs.test_go
  Steps
    ✓  5  Run make GO_ONLY=1 SKIP_GOLANGCI_LINT=1
    ✓  6  Run go test ./tsdb/ -test.tsdb-isolation=false
    ✗  7  Run make -C documentation/examples/remote_storage  ← failed here
    ○  8  Run make -C documentation/examples (skipped)
  Failed step  #7 Run make -C documentation/examples/remote_storage
    shell: sh -e {0}
    $ make -C documentation/examples/remote_storage
  Diagnosis  files out of date (a check produced a git diff) · exit code 2
  Log excerpt (10 lines around the first error in "Run make -C documentation/examples/remote_storage")
    │ >> running check for unused/missing packages in go.mod
    │ go mod tidy
    │ go: downloading github.com/oapi-codegen/nullable v1.1.0
    │ diff --git a/documentation/examples/remote_storage/go.mod b/documentation/examples/remote_storage/go.mod
    │ --- a/documentation/examples/remote_storage/go.mod
    │ +++ b/documentation/examples/remote_storage/go.mod
  Reproduction notes
    ! job runs inside container quay.io/prometheus/golang-builder:1.27-base
The log ends with hundreds of lines of go.sum diff. FailTrace centres the excerpt on the first error
line so you see the cause, go mod tidy changing go.mod, instead of the noise after it.
macOS and Linux, using the install script. It downloads the latest release for your platform and verifies its SHA-256 checksum:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ri4dH/failtrace/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
It installs to /usr/local/bin if that's writable, otherwise to ~/.local/bin. Set
FAILTRACE_INSTALL_DIR to choose, or FAILTRACE_VERSION=v0.1.0 to pin a release.
Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows (amd64 and arm64) are on the
releases page, with a checksums.txt.
With Go 1.24+:
go install github.com/Ri4dH/failtrace/cmd/failtrace@latest
From source:
git clone https://github.com/Ri4dH/failtrace
cd failtrace
go build -o bin/failtrace ./cmd/failtrace# All failed jobs in the latest attempt of a run
failtrace inspect https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/123456789
# A single job (the URL you get from clicking a job in the Actions UI)
failtrace inspect https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/123456789/job/987654321
# A specific attempt of a re-run workflow
failtrace inspect https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/123456789/attempts/2
# Show more log context, or emit JSON for scripts and other tools
failtrace inspect -n 60 <run-url>
failtrace inspect --json <run-url> | jq '.failed_jobs[0].failure'
Colour output turns off automatically when stdout is not a terminal, or when NO_COLOR is set.
FailTrace needs a GitHub token, even for public repositories, because the logs API requires one. It looks in this order:
- GITHUB_TOKEN
- GH_TOKEN
- gh auth token (if you use the GitHub CLI, this already works)
Private repositories need a token that can read Actions on that repo. GitHub Enterprise Server URLs work too:
the API base becomes https://<host>/api/v3.
- Run context: workflow, event, branch, commit, attempt.
- Job → workflow mapping: finds the job definition, including jobs named like
test (ubuntu-latest, 1.22) or Lint ${{ matrix.tool }}, and recovers the matrix values.
- Runner: the requested label and the actual runner image and version, from the log.
- Failed step: its definition (run, uses, with, env, shell, working directory). The command
shown is the one printed in the log, with expressions already filled in.
- Diagnosis: exit code, error annotations, failing test names (Go, pytest, Jest, Vitest, Cargo, RSpec), and a category:
- Reproduction notes: anything that makes a local repro harder. That means service containers, job containers, secrets the step uses, reusable workflows, and macOS or Windows runners.
It also explains edge cases instead of failing silently: runs that failed before any job started, dynamic workflows with no file in the repo, and logs that have expired.
failtrace plan works out how to reproduce the failed job locally and prints the plan. It doesn't run
anything yet.
failtrace plan https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/123456789
failtrace plan --job 987654321 <run-url>     # pick a job when several failed
failtrace plan --json <run-url>              # the full plan, including every env var
Real output for a failed pytest-dev/pytest job (trimmed):
Reproduction plan · pytest-dev/pytest
  Job        build (ubuntu-py311)  (jobs.build)
  Verdict    PARTIAL: can run, but the warnings below may make it differ from CI
  Image      ubuntu:26.04  linux/amd64
             matches the runner image ubuntu-26.04 20261111.196.1
  Commit     c484767
  Toolchains
    python   3.11.18    exact · asked for "3.11" · from actions/setup-python@6d4fd22
    uv       0.13.8     exact · from astral-sh/setup-uv@11f9893
  Steps
    1  checkout    Run actions/checkout@3d3c42e
                    pytest-dev/pytest @ c484767 (merge of 58b8dae into 50234b4)
    2  skip        Download Package
                    — downloads artifacts from another job
    3  toolchain   Set up Python 3.11
                    → install python 3.11.18
    4  composite   Run pytest-dev/pytest/.github/actions/setup-tox@c484767
                    — composite action; its steps follow
    5    toolchain   Run astral-sh/setup-uv@11f9893
                      → install uv 0.13.8
    6    run         $ if [ -n "$PYTHON_VERSION" ]; then  (+4 lines)
    7  run         Test with coverage  ← failed in CI
                    $ tox run -e py311-coverage --installpkg `find dist/*.tar.gz`
                    shell: /usr/bin/bash --noprofile --norc -e -o pipefail {0}
  Issues
    ! [step 2] actions/download-artifact@9000827 downloads artifacts produced by another job or run; files it provides will be missing locally
    i [step 1] CI tested the merge of PR head 58b8dae into base 50234b4 (merge commit c484767), not the PR branch alone; the plan checks out that merge commit
How the plan is built:
- The log is the source of truth for what ran. Scripts, shells and environment come from the step
headers GitHub prints, so ${{ matrix.* }} and other expressions are already filled in. Composite
actions show their inner steps.
- The exact commit CI tested. For pull requests that's a merge commit GitHub created, not your branch head. This is a common reason a failure "doesn't happen locally".
- The exact toolchain versions. "3.11" in the workflow becomes 3.11.18, read from the runner's
tool cache paths. When the log doesn't show a version, it reads version files such as go.mod (including toolchain), .nvmrc, .python-version, .tool-versions and packageManager in package.json.
- The right base image. A job container: is used as is. Otherwise it picks the Ubuntu version
matching the runner image the job actually got.
- What to skip and what to flag. Caches, uploads and coverage reporters are skipped. Downloaded artifacts, service containers, secrets, unknown actions, and tools used without a setup step (they were preinstalled on the runner) are reported as issues.
The verdict is ready (nothing known to be missing), partial (it can run, but some parts are
approximated or missing) or blocked (the failing step is an action, not a script, so it can't be replayed
yet).
Supported setup actions: actions/setup-go, setup-node, setup-python, setup-java, setup-dotnet,
ruby/setup-ruby, dtolnay/rust-toolchain, actions-rust-lang/setup-rust-toolchain,
pnpm/action-setup, pnpm/setup, astral-sh/setup-uv, oven-sh/setup-bun and denoland/setup-deno.
failtrace repro builds the plan and runs it in Docker, then compares the result with CI's failure.
failtrace repro <run-url>
failtrace repro --keep <run-url>                     # keep the container to poke around afterwards
API_TOKEN=... failtrace repro --secret API_TOKEN <run-url>
failtrace repro --toolchain node=20.11.1 <run-url>   # fill in or override a toolchain
failtrace repro --platform linux/arm64 <run-url>     # run natively on Apple silicon (faster, less exact)
failtrace repro --runs 10 <run-url>                  # is it flaky?
failtrace repro --shell <run-url>                    # debug inside the container afterwards
failtrace repro --report repro.md <run-url>          # Markdown report for an issue or PR
You need Docker (Docker Desktop, colima, OrbStack, …) and git.
Real output for a failed stretchr/testify run, where go vet failed
under Go oldstable. FailTrace resolved oldstable to the exact Go 1.26.9 build CI used, checked out the
PR merge commit CI tested, and replayed the steps:
$ failtrace repro --platform linux/arm64 https://github.com/stretchr/testify/actions/runs/39247781971
Reproducing stretchr/testify · build (oldstable) · plan ready
▶ Image       failtrace-env:08414601e6c4aef4 (cached)
▶ Workspace   stretchr/testify @ 9272105
▶ [3/5]       Run ./.ci.gogenerate.sh
  ✓ exit code 0 (17.7s)
▶ [4/5]       Run ./.ci.gofmt.sh
  ✓ exit code 0 (7.4s)
▶ [5/5]       Run ./.ci.govet.sh  ← failed in CI
    │ assert/assertion_compare_test.go:85:13: non-constant format string in call to (*testing.common).Errorf
    │ assert/assertion_compare_test.go:94:13: non-constant format string in call to (*testing.common).Errorf
  ✗ exit code 1 (10.7s)
✓ Reproduced: the step fails locally the same way it failed in CI
  • the same error: assert/assertion_compare_test.go:<n>:<n>: non-constant format string in call to (*testing.common).Errorf
                 CI                           Local
  Exit code      1                            1
  Failure        lint / format check          lint / format check
  Steps      4 passed · 1 failed (39s total)
  Image      failtrace-env:08414601e6c4aef4 linux/arm64
  Differences from CI
    - the image is plain ubuntu:24.04 with common runner packages; GitHub's runner image has far more preinstalled
    - steps run as root; on GitHub's runners they run as the `runner` user with passwordless sudo
    - running linux/arm64, but CI ran linux/amd64
Without --platform, the job runs as linux/amd64 like CI did. On an Apple silicon Mac that means
emulation: the same reproduction took about 9 minutes instead of 40 seconds, with the same verdict.
What happens:
- Environment image. The plan's base image, plus the packages every GitHub Ubuntu runner has
(git, curl, build tools, python3, jq, sudo, …), plus the toolchains. Go, Node and Python are the same
builds setup-go, setup-node and setup-python download, installed under /opt/hostedtoolcache where CI keeps them. uv, pnpm and Rust are installed from their releases. The image is tagged by a hash
of its contents, so it's only built once per environment.
- Workspace. The exact commit CI tested is fetched on your machine the way actions/checkout does
it, with the same fetch depth, and mounted at the same path as on the runner
(/home/runner/work/<repo>/<repo>, or /__w/... for container jobs). If GitHub has since replaced a
pull request's merge commit, the merge is recreated locally.
- Services. Service containers start in the job container's network namespace, so localhost:5432 and postgres:5432 both work, and FailTrace waits for their health checks.
- Steps. Run steps replay in order with the shell, environment and working directory CI used.
$GITHUB_ENV and $GITHUB_PATH carry over between steps. The failing step's output streams live.
- Verdict. 
  - reproduced: the same tests failed, or the same error or exit code.
  - different-failure
  - not-reproduced: the step passed locally.
  - diverged: an earlier step failed locally, so the failing step never ran.
  - flaky: with --runs, the step failed in some runs but not all.
A list of known differences from CI comes with every verdict.
The setup steps run once, then the failing step runs N times in the same container, so repeats are
cheap. If it fails only some of the time, the verdict is flaky ("the step failed in 3 of 10 runs").
Go's test cache is bypassed for these runs (GOFLAGS=-count=1). Otherwise go test would replay a cached
pass and hide the flakiness.
When the run finishes, --shell opens a shell where the failing step ran: same directory, environment,
toolchains and services. It prints the command that re-runs the step:
▶ Shell       inside the container at step 5 (Run ./.ci.govet.sh); type exit to finish
              re-run the step with: bash -e /home/runner/work/_temp/failtrace/step-5.sh
If an earlier step diverged, the shell opens at that step instead. The container is removed when you exit,
unless you pass --keep.
--report repro.md writes a Markdown report to paste into an issue or pull request. It includes the
verdict, a CI-vs-local table, environment, differences, every step's result, and the output of the failing
step from both sides. --report - prints it instead of the terminal summary. See
docs/example-report.md, generated from the stretchr/testify run above with
--runs 3.
Safety. repro runs the repository's code, including code from a pull request, inside a container on
your machine. The container sees only the workspace, has no access to your home directory or the Docker
socket, and gets no secrets unless you pass them with --secret NAME. The value is read from your
environment, so it never appears in your shell history or the process list. Only reproduce runs whose
code you're comfortable executing.
Limitations. These are reported instead of silently ignored:
- A failing step that is an action rather than a script can't be replayed (verdict blocked).
- Windows and macOS jobs are only approximated in Linux.
- Steps run as root, where CI uses the runner user.
- The runner image's many preinstalled tools aren't all present.
- linux/amd64 jobs are emulated on ARM machines.
- Artifacts from other jobs aren't available.
- inspect: diagnose a failed run from its URL
- plan: turn the failed job into a local reproduction plan: base image, exact commit, toolchain
versions, env, steps to replay
- repro: run the plan in Docker and compare the result with CI
-  Reports: --report writes a Markdown report with the verdict and the differences from CI
-  Flaky detection: --runs N repeats the failing step and reports flaky
- --shell: drop into the container at the failing step
- Releases: prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows, and a checksum-verifying install script
-  Homebrew and gh extension: brew install and gh failtrace <run-url>
-  Replaying common actions: translate actions such as golangci-lint-action into the commands
they run, so failures in them can be reproduced too
go test ./...                                     # unit tests (no network or Docker needed)
go test -race ./...
go vet ./...
go test -tags integration ./internal/repro/       # runs real containers; needs Docker
goreleaser release --snapshot --clean             # build release archives locally, publish nothing
CI runs all of the above on every pull request. To publish a release, push a version tag (git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0); release.yml builds and uploads the binaries.
Project layout:
cmd/failtrace/      CLI entry point
internal/cli/       commands and flags
internal/runurl/    run URL parsing and validation
internal/github/    minimal GitHub REST client and token lookup
internal/joblog/    job log parsing, failure extraction and classification
internal/workflow/  workflow YAML parsing, job/step/matrix matching
internal/inspect/   puts it all together into a report
internal/plan/      builds reproduction plans (image, commit, toolchains, env, steps)
internal/toolchain/ resolves toolchains to the builds setup-* actions use
internal/docker/    runs containers through the docker CLI
internal/repro/     executes a plan and compares the result with CI
internal/report/    terminal rendering
Issues and pull requests are welcome. The most useful contributions right now:
- Failed runs that FailTrace gets wrong. Open an issue with the run URL and what you expected.
- New failure signatures: test runners, package managers and compilers that aren't detected yet.
These live in internal/joblog/analyze.go and need a test case.
- More known actions: setup actions (internal/plan/toolchains.go) and actions that are safe to
skip locally (internal/plan/actions.go). Each one is a single table entry.

articles.title: Absolute Batman can save DC Studios
articles.body:
With James Gunn and Peter Safran out as the co-heads of DC Studios following Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, it’s unclear what will become of the cinematic universe that was building around movies like last year’s Superman. Though Gunn’s Man of Tomorrowfeature might still come out, it seems like his larger vision for the DC Universe may be tossed out by DC Studios’ newly appointed CEO, Jeremy Latcham. Gunn was taking his time fleshing out the DCU with relatively less high-profile characters like Peacemaker, Supergirl, and Clayface. But Latcham has reportedly received a mandate from Skydance CEO David Ellison to fast-track a new version of the Justice League featuring more popular heroes like Wonder Woman and the Green Lantern.
Absolute Batman can save DC Studios
Skydance’s cinematic superhero universe could get back on track through DC’s progressive Absolute Universe comics.
This drastic shift in priorities will likely change what the DCU looks like in the coming years as Skydance attempts to parlay its comics IP into projects that can help it get on top of the $80 billion of debt the company is now responsible for after acquiring WBD. Ellison’s instinct to whip out the A-list superheroes is probably right from a business perspective. Most casual DC movie fans are more interested in stories about the Trinity than obscure characters like Gorilla Grodd. But after two iffy attempts at creating interconnected DC movie franchises, that audience might not have much of an appetite for yet another full-on reboot.
Rather than starting from scratch, DC Studios should probably keep some of the things that worked well during Gunn and Safran’s tenure, like presenting Superman as a compassionate person with a strong moral compass. But if the studio really wants to take this franchise in a new direction that gets people excited, it should also be thinking about tapping into the energy of some of DC’s most successful recent comics. Though the WBD merger prompted Skydance to begin laying off almost 2,000 employees last month, DC Comics — which Skydance gained control of as part of the deal — was reportedly left unscathed because the publishing arm’s business has been performing surprisingly well. Much of that success seems to have been driven by strong sales of comics created by DC’s Absolute Universe imprint.
Launched in 2024, the Absolute Universe comics reimagine DC’s heroes and villains as wildly different versions of their classic selves. Absolute Wonder Woman is a witch raised in Hell, Absolute Superman first arrives on Earth as a teenager who remembers his childhood on Krypton, and Absolute Batman is a working-class civil engineer rather than a socialite born into immense wealth. The Absolute characters’ worldviews and approaches to enacting justice are all distinct from their mainstream universe counterparts. But as much as the Absolute comics diverge from established canon, they each capture the essence of what makes their central characters iconic pillars of the DC brand.
Wonder Woman aside, there have been so many cinematic portrayals of DC characters based on their classic selves that it has often seemed like Warner Bros. was stuck in a kind of rut. There have been slight stylistic differences between the various big-screen iterations of Superman and Batman over the years, but for the most part, they have all come across as the products of a studio that’s averse to trying new things.
Absolute Batman is compelling because it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics.
That’s part of what made Matt Reeves’ The Batman— which didn’t bother to rehash Bruce Wayne’s tragic origin story — feel somewhat like a breath of fresh air when it debuted in 2022. Robert Pattinson will reprise his role as the Dark Knight in The Batman Part II, but it’s not really clear whether that version of the character will have any bearing on the DCU’s future.
Between Reeves’ Batman films existing in their own universe (similar to Todd Phillips’ Joker features) and Pattinson presumably being busy now that he’s been cast as Amazon’s new James Bond, it doesn’t seem likely that that version of the character will be incorporated into the DCU. Ellison obviously intends to put out more projects featuring Batman, though, and DC Studios could tell a riveting story if it took some cues from the hero’s Absolute incarnation. What makes Absolute Batman such a compelling series is the way it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics. In those books, Bruce Wayne is part of Gotham’s marginalized underclass, while the Joker is a moneyed elite whose villainy is highlighted in the way he manipulates various industries.
This inversion puts Absolute Batman in a position to operate as a vigilante with a much deeper connection to the ordinary people he has sworn to protect. Monstrous supervillains like Poison Ivy and Bane are still major threats, but the comics also spend time pitting Absolute Batman against more ordinary evils like corrupt police departments infested with white nationalists fixated on terrorizing minorities. Absolute Batman’s progressive political overtones might not gel with Ellison’s personal sensibilities, and the comic’s brutality probably doesn’t align with Latcham’s approach to making films. But Absolute Batman’s phenomenal sales have made it abundantly clear that readers are enjoying these stories, which is likely a big part why DC Studios announced earlier this year that it has plans to produce an animated series based on the comics.
Those plans might change in the wake of Skydance acquiring WBD, but an Absolute Batman series would give DC Studios an organic way to introduce the character into its tentpole films. Having characters jump back and forth between TV and the big screen was one of the stronger ideas Gunn introduced to the DCU, and it’s a strategy that could continue to benefit DC Studios under Latcham’s leadership. Turning Absolute Batman into the next flagship Bruce Wayne would be a bold move on Skydance’s part. But if the studio really wants to prove that this megamerger was the right decision, it needs to show the public that it has the guts to take exciting chances.

articles.title: Just Because You Can, Doesn't Mean You Should: Re-Evaluating Galera Node Weights
articles.body:
We all know that when using a cluster based on Galera (Codership) such as Percona XtraDB Cluster (PXC), it is recommended to deploy an odd number of nodes.
The generic answer to this recommendation is that otherwise the risk of having an inconsistent cluster (like split-brain) is higher. (see Get started with Percona XtraDB Cluster – Percona XtraDB Cluster )
As a reminder, when split-brain occurs, a cluster will stop accepting queries, which is what a safe solution should do while waiting for the DBA to review and decide which of the two nodes is the leader. I do not even want to describe the infamous wsrep_provider_options=”pc.ignore_sb = yes”, which has been the cause of many, many nights spent trying to reconcile the corrupted datasets. If you have it, remove it.
However, in Galera, we also have the setting wsrep_provider_options=”pc.weight=N”. With it, we can define a specific weight in the quorum calculation for each node. 
The question naturally arises: if we can assign a different weight to each node, why can’t we have an even number of nodes and assign them different weights? 
The answer to the question is simple, yes, we can.
What is not simple is to identify who should have a different weight and how to distribute it.
To understand the problem, we need to review how the quorum is calculated (I have touched on the topic long ago here TusaCentral – Geographic replication and quorum Calculation in MySQL/Galera) and what a View is.
In Percona XtraDB Cluster (PXC) and Galera, a View (or cluster view) is the agreed-upon membership of the cluster at any specific moment in time. It represents the exact list of nodes that are currently connected, synchronized, and actively communicating with each other.
Whenever a node joins the cluster, leaves gracefully, or drops out due to a network failure, the remaining connected nodes negotiate a new View and assign it a unique View ID.
Its relationship to the Primary Component (PC) is based on quorum:
Essentially, a View defines who is currently connected to each other, while the Primary Component is the specific View that has enough members to safely keep the database running.
The formula for calculating the quorum is:
Σ p·w < 2·(Σ m·w + Σ l·w)
Where:
p = members of the last PRIMARY view 
l = members that left gracefully (LEFT)
m = members of the component being evaluated
w = pc.weight (0–255).
In short, the total weight of the previous Primary view must be less than twice the weight of the members of the new component plus the weight of the members that left gracefully.  To be clear, a crashed / unreachable node (DOWN or in another partition) still counts in Σ p·w, so it pushes the threshold up. 
A graceful leave (LEFT), instead, is credited to the new component. Also, any node that was not in the last PC is dropped from calculation, so a node that has just joined or rejoined contributes nothing to this check.
Look for the function:
(repo https://github.com/percona/galera/tree/a6b54d887d58bae43ae3f46f5696195329405b7e)
Now let’s assume that we have a cluster of 4 nodes, there are many possible combinations where things will work and where instead they will hit us badly.
The most common is the split-brain scenario:
To prevent this, we may decide to use one node with different weight:
Here we go, problem solved… really?
No, because changing weights may cause other issues, for example if we calculate the weights wrongly with respect to the number of nodes:
In this case one single node could bring down the whole cluster.
Of course, if we perform standard operations, or crashes happen in cascade and the cluster has time to rebuild the Primary Component, all will work well:
The problem is that:
The real question is not if we can do it but whether it is worth it: does using an odd number of nodes help or not?
The answer is partly.
Odd nodes get rid of the exact-tie case in the simple situation. They don’t completely stop the cluster losing PRIMARY state.
What matters is the parity of the total weight, not the node count. 
A tie happens when present = partitioned, which means the counted weight (Σw(PC) − Left) splits exactly in half. 
That is only possible when the counted weight is even. So:
Where odd nodes still lose PRIMARY:
In practice: aim for an odd total weight in the PC and use a third site or an arbitrator for multi-DC setups. Even then, a cluster that has already shrunk can become even again, so the last-two-nodes tie can’t be designed away.
Only pc.ignore_sb or a manual bootstrap gets past it. But you do not want to go there.
Given this, and given that what counts is NOT the number of nodes but the balance in the weight calculation, is using weights the right way to compensate?
Well, this may be my personal opinion, but in my experience, weights make the cluster harder to manage, and the stability they add is narrow.
A weight-2 node acts like two nodes that always fail together. Four nodes weighted 2,1,1,1 behave like a 5-node cluster where two of the nodes share one box. 
We trade a split-brain tie for a single point of fate:
The set of survivable failures shifts rather than grows. We still tolerate only one arbitrary failure plus some specific splits.
What weights add to day-to-day operations:
Simple to most complex for the same goal:
Weights don’t make the cluster generally more stable, and they add operational complexity. They make sense as a deliberate tiebreaker, not as a fix for even node counts.
I stand by the evergreen KISS motto: Keep It Simple and Straightforward.
Having a PXC cluster with more than 3 nodes makes sense in very few cases, and only to scale reads or if you plan to kill 2 nodes at the same time on a cluster of 5.
Given the significant complications the increase of nodes or the use of weight brings, I do not really see why someone in a healthy state of mind should look for trouble.
Just because it can be done, it doesn’t mean “do it”, especially if the gain is minimal and the complexity increases.
Do yourself a favor: keep your cluster to the minimum, to what is really needed and do not try to stretch it. You will save yourself from spending miserable nights doing cluster recovery or worse data reconciliation.
Great MySQL to everyone.

articles.title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation
The Magic of Partial Evaluation
Disney’s new Star Wars animatronics interact with guests using AI
articles.body:
As advanced and lifelike as the animatronic characters at Disney parks have become, they typically either stick to predefined movements and routines, or there’s an out of sight puppeteer helping make their behavior appear more spontaneous. That could soon change as Walt Disney Imagineering R&D has revealed three new Audio-Animatronic prototypes that rely on Amazon’s AWS cloud and AI capabilities to respond in unique ways to guest interactions in real-time.
Disney’s new Star Wars animatronics interact with guests using AI
The three Anzellans each have distinct personalities and respond to guest interactions using hidden cameras and mics.
The three animatronics, named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a, and Jibu Bre’a, are based on the Star Wars alien characters called the Anzellans that were featured in The Mandalorian and Grogu film released earlier this year. The tiny bots will make their first public appearance in Las Vegas later this month where attendees of the AWS re:Invent conference will have a chance to interact with them, although the characters, and the technology powering them, could eventually find its way into Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge and other attractions at Disney’s parks.
Unlike Disney’s Olaf robot that recently debuted, there’s no one secretly using a Steam Deck gaming handheld to bring the Anzellans to life. The animatronics instead each have hidden cameras and microphones they use to capture guest movements and verbal interactions which are processed by multiple AI models running on AWS cloud servers. One “fast-decision model” generates quick responses such as the animatronics quickly making eye contact so it appears as if they’re paying attention, while larger models plan out longer interactions.
However, the Anzellans movements and verbal responses aren’t generated on the fly by AI. Every movement and line of dialogue that’s selected and triggered by the models is prewritten by Disney Imagineers to ensure the animations stay true to each character, including unique personality quirks for each one. Although AI helps guide their actions, the Anzellans never deviate from the script.

articles.title: Lakegres: Vector search on existing Open/Hudi/Iceberg tables
articles.body:
TL;DR
- Problem: Vector search is a standard feature of application databases. Lake and warehouse data still has to be copied into a separate search system before an agent can search it.
- Why now: Agents query all of a company’s data. Most of that data is stored in open tables that are 100 to 1,000 times larger than any application database.
- What we built: Lakegres now provides vector search through an index stored inside existing and new Hudi and Iceberg tables.
- How it works: The index is derived metadata: build or drop it without rewriting the table’s data files. It groups vectors into clusters, stores compact quantized codes, and is maintained by the same commits that write the table.
- Why it matters: On 247 million vectors, warm queries return in 63.5 ms at the median. Lakegres is about 10 times faster than Databricks AI Search at the warm median.
Today we are announcing vector search in Onehouse Lakegres, with a native index stored inside existing and new open tables. You can search embeddings through a Postgres endpoint on the same tables you already have in your data lake. The index and data are managed in open formats in your own bucket.
Vector search stopped at the application database
A few years ago, adding vector search required a separate database. Postgres now has pgvector, OpenSearch has k-NN, and MySQL, Oracle, MongoDB and SQL Server have their own implementations. Databricks also offers vector search in Lakebase Search. Similarity search has become a standard index type for application data.
Most of the data an agent needs to query is in the lakehouse. Support transcripts, logs, documents, product catalogs and years of event history are stored in open tables on object storage. These datasets are 100 to 1,000 times larger than a typical Postgres instance. To search them with any of those databases, you have to copy the data into the database first. Copying lake-scale datasets into a relational database just to search their vectors is an absurd requirement. You end up paying to store the data twice and operating a pipeline to keep the copies in sync.
Yesterday, we announced unstructured data processing on Onehouse, which parses documents, images and video and stores their embeddings in open tables. Lakegres can now index and search those vectors, so agents can query that unstructured content alongside the business records already in the lakehouse.
How the market searches lake data today
Lakehouse and warehouse vendors have also added vector search. Each vendor below stores the index outside the open table, in a service or format that requires its own engine to read.
These vendors advocate open table formats while keeping their search indexes in closed formats. If you move to another engine, you have to rebuild every index in that vendor’s format, even though the underlying tables are open.
Why database techniques stop at lake scale
Most production vector search today runs on OpenSearch or Postgres. Both offer HNSW (OpenSearch implementation, pgvector implementation), a graph index that performs well when the entire graph fits in memory. AWS’s own sizing formula for OpenSearch is 1.1 × (4 × dimensions + 8 × m) bytes of RAM per vector. Our benchmark table has 247 million vectors at 1,024 dimensions. With m set to 16, that comes to about 1.15 TB of memory for one table, and about 46 TB at 10 billion vectors.
A pgvector HNSW index in Postgres also has to stay in shared buffers or the page cache to be fast, and latency degrades sharply once the working set exceeds RAM. Graph traversal is also a poor match for object storage, because each hop is a small random read. These designs work well for application databases with tens of millions of vectors. A data lake can be several orders of magnitude larger.
LinkedIn reported an exabyte across its Hadoop clusters in 2021. Uber’s lake holds 350 petabytes and ingests 6 trillion rows a day. Pinterest runs a 500-petabyte lake on Iceberg, and Netflix describes its Iceberg warehouse as exabyte scale. Embedding even a small fraction of these datasets produces billions of vectors. Keeping that many vectors in RAM is too expensive for most teams.
Training-data curation also needs large-scale similarity search. Post-training workflows can use it to select relevant examples and remove near-duplicates across large pools of candidate data. Repeated searches make cost per search matter as much as latency.
VAST, which supplies storage for AI training, uses a clustered vector index on flash in its distributed Element Store. Its launch material describes memory-resident indexes as prohibitively expensive at tens or hundreds of billions of vectors. turbopuffer also uses storage-based clustering. Lakegres applies this approach to existing Hudi and Iceberg tables through an open index.
What we built
Lakegres stores the vector index in the table’s metadata, in the same bucket as the data files. Commits that insert, update or delete rows also update the index. This keeps the index consistent with the table without a separate sync job or a second copy of the vectors. To our knowledge, this is the only available open vector search index for existing Hudi and Iceberg tables that is maintained with table writes and leaves the data files unchanged.
Iceberg support builds on the Hudi-backed indexing work in Apache XTable (Incubating). We developed the design in the open with engineers from Uber and Walmart to support their planet-scale tables. The open RFC documents the storage layout, query path and consistency model.
The design is settled and ships in Lakegres today; the Hudi implementation is being upstreamed and XTable is in release-candidate testing ahead of OSS releases that other engines can integrate.
Lakegres accepts queries over the Postgres wire protocol, so any Postgres client or agent framework can run a similarity search in SQL. The same endpoint already serves analytical scans, indexed point lookups and text search on those tables.
How it works
Add or drop the index without rewriting the table
The vector index is derived metadata. You can build it on an existing Hudi or Iceberg table with a vector column without rewriting the underlying data files. You can experiment with an index, rebuild it with different settings, or drop it when you no longer need it. Existing analytical queries continue to work. Trying vector search costs you an index build and its storage.
You do not have to move from Parquet to another file format like Lance or Vortex just to get vector search. Lakegres also already queries Lance and Vortex files while keeping the open table format the same. You can choose a file format for its storage and read characteristics independently of adding a vector index.
The base table stores the full vectors alongside the other columns. The index stores the smaller structures needed to find candidate rows: cluster centroids, quantizer state and packed index entries. These structures are stored in the table’s metadata and grouped into an index generation. Each query resolves a table snapshot and an active generation before reading the data, so it uses a compatible set of index structures throughout.
Clusters divide the search space into bounded reads
At build time, k-means groups vectors around representative points called centroids. Each vector is assigned to a cluster and encoded relative to its centroid using RaBitQ quantization. The encoding uses a fixed random rotation and compact codes at 1 to 8 bits per dimension, with 4 bits as the default. The stored codes support L2, cosine and dot-product distance calculations.
Clusters are divided into posting segments, with each segment stored in one metadata file group. Within a segment, roughly 1,000 to 4,000 vector entries are packed into a posting block, targeting about 512 KB. A posting contains the compressed scoring information, record key and a locator for the underlying row. Grouping them into blocks avoids creating billions of individual metadata records and lets the query read a cluster’s entries as contiguous key ranges.
Each block contains separate arrays for sign bits, extra precision bits, correction factors, row locators, dictionaries and record keys. The first scoring pass decodes the sign bits and factors. Later passes decode extra bits and row identities only for surviving candidates. The reader fetches the block as one record, then selectively decodes its arrays to reduce scoring work.
A query narrows the candidates before it fetches full vectors
Lakegres first compares the query vector with the centroids and probes the nearest clusters. The nprobes setting controls how many clusters it opens. Probing more clusters generally improves recall at the cost of more work. Within those clusters, a first pass uses one-bit estimates and error bounds to discard candidates that cannot beat the current shortlist. A second pass uses the remaining bits to refine the surviving candidates.
Before returning results, the reader validates candidate keys against the record index at the query’s snapshot. Deleted candidates are removed and moved records are resolved to their current location. Approximate mode ranks the candidates with their compact codes. Optional exact re-ranking reads the shortlisted vectors from the base table and computes their full distances. Exact re-ranking improves the ordering within the candidate set. The search still examines only the selected clusters.
The index stays up to date as the table changes
Each write adds small updates to the index. When a vector changes, the writer marks its old index entry as deleted and adds a new entry. When a row moves, the writer updates its location in the index. Queries read the packed blocks and these updates together. They use the latest entry for each record. Compaction periodically merges the updates into the blocks.
Before searching, the reader checks the table’s commit history. It verifies that the index includes the writes required by the query’s snapshot. A stale or incompatible index cannot serve the query. Depending on the configuration, the query either returns an error or scans the table for exact results.
You can rebuild the index while queries continue to run. The concurrency protocol coordinates table writes, index catch-up and snapshot reads so writers can keep committing while readers continue using a consistent index. The rebuild creates a new index version alongside the current one. It also picks up table writes made during the rebuild. Once the new version is ready, a single metadata commit makes it available to queries. Queries use the current version until the new version is online atomically. They never read a partially built index.
Benchmarks
We used Cohere’s public multilingual Wikipedia embedding dataset. Our table contains 247,154,006 passages, approximately 247M vectors, with 1,024-dimensional embeddings generated by Cohere Embed v3. The table occupies about 1 TB on S3.
We designed Lakegres vector search for tables that grow to billions of vectors. We therefore compare against Databricks AI Search’s storage-optimized tier, its offering for large datasets. Its standard tier has a documented capacity of roughly 320M vectors at 768 dimensions, equivalent to about 240M at the 1,024 dimensions used here.
We ran the same workload on Lakegres and Databricks AI Search, the most directly comparable service for lake data. Each system ran the same 200 queries for the 10 nearest neighbors, one at a time. Recall was scored against exact brute-force results.
For warm queries, Lakegres returned results in 63.5 ms at p50, 67.9 ms at p90 and 75.3 ms at p99. Databricks AI Search took 655 ms, 876 ms and 1,209 ms, respectively. Cold p50 latency was 536.2 ms for Lakegres and 8,242 ms for AI Search. Recall@10 was 0.95 for Lakegres and 0.952 for AI Search.
Warm queries benefit from partially cached index data. Queries read the posting blocks for selected clusters, fetching blocks from storage when they are not cached. The full vector dataset stays in the table and does not need to fit in memory.
Lakegres uses a configurable compute cluster. Databricks AI Search serves a separate index through a serverless endpoint, with capacity automatically sized for the indexed data.
Lakegres ran on five m8gd.4xlarge executor nodes and one r8gd.4xlarge driver. AI Search ran on six storage-optimized units with one replica, and its hardware is not visible to customers. We used Databricks’ server-side latency measurements for AI Search and client-side psql timings for Lakegres. The two measurements therefore cover different parts of query execution. In a preliminary standard-tier test on a smaller, 10-million-vector table, the index build ran at about 70,000 rows a minute before we stopped it; we did not measure query latency on that tier.
Lakegres is about 10 times faster at the warm median and 15 times faster cold. The AWS instances cost about $5.79/hour at US East on-demand rates, excluding Onehouse fees; the six AI Search units cost $7.68/hour. These figures show the modest infrastructure budget behind the Lakegres result. They are not a total-cost comparison.
We expect similar query latency on multi-billion-vector tables as we scale out Lakegres. This run used just five Spark executors plus a driver. As a table grows, we can increase the number of index clusters and distribute posting-block reads and scoring across more workers. Each query still searches selected clusters, and workers can fetch the required blocks from storage without loading the entire index into memory. This gives us control over the work per worker as the dataset grows. We will publish results on much larger vector datasets in follow-up blogs.
In a separate index-build benchmark, building the index took 18 minutes on Lakegres and about 3 hours 10 minutes on AI Search. Lakegres builds the index on the lakehouse’s elastic compute, so you can increase the cluster size to build it faster. AI Search provides no control over build cluster size and reports progress only as a percentage.

Get started
Create the index with a CREATE INDEX statement. These are the options we used for the benchmark table.
CREATE INDEX embedding_idx ON wiki_passages
USING VECTOR (embedding)
OPTIONS (
  `vector.metric` = 'l2',
  `vector.num_clusters` = '65536',
  `vector.rabitq.bits` = '4'
);
To search, call the table function from any Postgres client. It returns the nearest rows and their distances. The nprobes option controls how many clusters the query opens, which is the main tradeoff between latency and recall.
SELECT id, _distance
FROM vector_search(
  'wiki_passages', 'embedding',
  ARRAY[0.12, -0.03, 0.44],   -- the query embedding, shortened here
  10, 'l2', 'ivf_rabitq_mdt',
  'vector.query.nprobes=128'
);
Where we’re headed
Most of the remaining latency difference from the fastest dedicated systems comes from work outside the index. Roughly 20 to 25 ms of each query is spent in Spark, in planning and task scheduling, before any index block is read. We saw the same fixed overhead, in the tens of milliseconds, when testing Trino and other lake engines. These engines were built to plan large scans. We have designed a way to remove this overhead from index lookups and plan to implement it next.
The first release supports filtering through partition pruning. It does not support arbitrary predicates combined with nearest-neighbor search. If the cluster layout drifts from the data, you can rebuild the index while queries continue, then activate the new generation atomically.
Conclusion
Agents need four kinds of queries from a data platform: analytical scans, indexed point lookups, text search and vector search. Lakegres now serves all four from one copy of your open tables, through one Postgres endpoint, as the platform guide describes.
